It behaves much like column-at-a-time: 60 MB of intermediates spill out of cache and execution becomes memory-bound
explain: 1,000,000 x 60 bytes is 60 MB, far beyond a 2 MB cache, so every intermediate is written to and re-read from RAM, like MonetDB/MIL. Overhead is already negligible by about 1,000 values; going bigger only adds cache misses.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes
question: In lesson 1's -O0 listing, sum loads and stores s on every trip. Which steps remove that memory traffic at -O2?
options: Vectorization
Loop-invariant code motion
Promoting the stack slot to an SSA value (mem2reg), then register allocation
Dead code elimination
explain: The traffic exists because s has a stack slot. mem2reg replaces the slot's loads and stores with SSA values and a phi, and the register allocator then keeps that value in rax. LICM moves invariant work, but s changes every trip; DCE deletes unused work, but s is used.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
question: A teammate adds `-flto` only to the final link command; all .o files were compiled without it. What happens?
options: Full LTO across all files
The link fails
Only main.c is re-optimized
No cross-file optimization: the .o files contain only machine code
explain: LTO works on the IR stored in object files. Objects compiled without -flto contain only machine code, so the link-time optimizer has nothing to work with. -flto (and -O) must be given at compile time too.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
question: A model returns a response with three tool_use blocks: left_click, type, screenshot. What should the harness send back?
options: Only the screenshot image, since that is the observation the model needs
One tool_result per tool_use block, in one user message, matched by tool_use_id
Nothing yet: wait for the model to send each action in a separate turn
A text summary of the three actions written by the harness
explain: The docs require one tool_result for every tool_use block, all in the next user message and matched by tool_use_id. A request that leaves any block unanswered is rejected. The click and type results can be a short OK; the screenshot result is the image.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
question: Which verification step best catches a failed "save the report as PDF" task?
options: Checking that the file exists at the expected path with a PDF header and non-zero size
Asking the model whether it thinks it saved the file
Checking that the last action was a click on the Save button
Taking a screenshot and confirming the Save dialog is no longer open
explain: A closed dialog or a Save click does not prove a file was written (the dialog may have been cancelled, or the path may be wrong). Checking the resulting state is what OSWorld's evaluators do and what the vendor docs recommend before reporting success.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Preemption bounds, weak memory and what loom cannot see
question: A loom test of a seqlock (a lock where readers retry if a writer bumped a sequence counter) that uses `store(.., SeqCst)` panics, but you are confident the algorithm is correct under C11. What is the most likely explanation?
options: loom found a real bug that hardware hides
The preemption bound was set too high
loom does not support SeqCst at all and always panics
loom treats SeqCst loads and stores as AcqRel, so it may explore executions that SeqCst forbids, producing a false alarm
explain: The README lists this exact limitation. Check whether the failing execution relies on a reordering SeqCst would forbid; fence(SeqCst) is modeled correctly, plain SeqCst accesses are weakened.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: The boundary condition and the c_skip, c_out parameterization
question: A teammate drops c_skip and c_out and uses f(x, t) = F(x, t) directly, trained with the consistency loss only. What is the main risk?
options: Training becomes slower but converges to the same solution
Nothing ties the outputs to data, so a constant output such as f = 0 minimizes the loss
The model can no longer be sampled in one step
The ODE solver in the teacher becomes unstable
explain: Self-consistency only says outputs agree along a trajectory; a constant function agrees everywhere. The boundary condition f(x, eps) = x anchors the chain to real data, and the paper states it precludes the trivial solution. (Song et al. also allow a piecewise version that returns x at t = eps, but some anchor is required.)

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
question: Your service keeps each key linearizable on its own, using a separate replica group per key. A teammate worries that a history mixing single-key operations on many keys is therefore not linearizable as a whole. What does locality say?
options: Per-key linearizability implies the whole history of single-key operations is linearizable
The teammate is right; you need a global lock across groups
Locality only holds for sequential consistency
It depends on clock synchronization between groups
explain: Herlihy and Wing's Theorem 1: a history is linearizable if and only if each object's sub-history is. This covers single-key operations. An atomic operation that touches two keys at once is a different object (or a transaction), which locality does not cover.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
question: A cache tier uses hash mod N with 10 servers. One server crashes and clients switch to mod 9. Roughly what fraction of cache lookups now go to a server that does not hold the key?
options: About 10%, only the dead server's keys
About 50%
About 90%
None, because the hash function did not change
explain: Going from 10 to 9 has the same structure as 9 to 10: only 1 in 10 hash values gives the same remainder mod 9 and mod 10, so about 90% of keys move. Losing one server makes nearly the whole cache miss at once, which is exactly the kind of stampede that knocks over the database behind it.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
question: Which requirement is the best candidate for a soft constraint rather than a hard filter?
options: Candidate has the security clearance the contract legally requires
Candidate has not opted out of being contacted by recruiters
Candidate profile is in the recruiter's licensed country
Candidate lives within commuting distance of the office
explain: Distance is a matter of degree: 12 km is a bit worse than 3 km, not a disqualification. Legal, contractual and consent rules are binary and must never be traded for other strengths, so they belong in hard filters.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
question: You add a fifth job E with the same three slots. How many complete assignments must generate and test consider now?
options: 84, since one variable adds three new values
243, since the count multiplies by the domain size
324, since it multiplies by the number of variables
125, which is five jobs raised to three slots
explain: The count is $d^n$. Going from $n=4$ to $n=5$ with $d=3$ multiplies it by 3: $81 \times 3 = 243$. Each new variable multiplies the space, which is why enumeration collapses so quickly.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
question: A constraint says 0.3 x + 0.5 y <= 4 with x, y integers. How should it go into CP-SAT?
options: Pass it as written; CP-SAT converts floats internally to exact rationals
Round each coefficient to the nearest integer: 0 x + 1 y <= 4
Multiply through by 10: 3 x + 5 y <= 40
Replace it with x + y <= 4, which is equivalent
explain: The docs state CP-SAT works over the integers, so non-integer coefficients must be scaled by a large enough integer. Multiplying both sides by 10 keeps exactly the same feasible set. Rounding changes the constraint, and option D drops the weights entirely.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
question: A pod spec uses `image: shop/web:1.4`. The image was signed and scanned when 1.4 was first pushed. What risk remains?
options: The tag can later be pointed at different bytes, which were never scanned, and no signature check runs unless admission enforces it
The kubelet re-verifies signatures on every pull by default
Tags expire after 30 days
None, because it was signed
explain: Signing at push time does nothing unless something verifies at deploy time, and a tag can be moved. Pin the digest and enforce signature verification in admission.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
question: A RoleBinding in namespace dev references the ClusterRole secret-reader. Where can the subject read Secrets?
options: Nowhere; RoleBindings cannot reference ClusterRoles
In every namespace, because it is a ClusterRole
Only in kube-system
Only in dev, because a RoleBinding grants within its own namespace
explain: The RBAC docs give this exact example: a RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole, and the binding's namespace decides where the rights apply. Only a ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
question: After applying default-deny-all, every app fails with name resolution errors, but the allow rules between apps look right. What is missing?
options: Nothing; restart the pods
An ingress rule on the DNS pods
An egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the cluster DNS pods
A ClusterRoleBinding for DNS
explain: Default deny for egress also blocks DNS queries, as the docs warn. Add an egress allow to the cluster DNS service on port 53.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
question: Which event would appear in the Kubernetes audit log but not necessarily in Falco?
options: A write to /etc/ld.so.preload
A shell spawned in a container through an anonymous kubelet
A service account listing all Secrets through the API server
A miner connecting to a pool
explain: Listing Secrets is an API request, recorded by the audit log, and produces no unusual process activity on a node for a syscall sensor to see. The others happen on nodes, outside the API server.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: cgroup v2: cpu.max throttling and memory.max kills
question: Which pairing correctly matches a cgroup v2 limit to what happens when a workload pushes past it?
options: cpu.max kills the process; memory.max throttles it
cpu.max stalls the threads until the next period; memory.max reclaims first, then OOM kills inside the cgroup
Both throttle: allocations are slowed to the configured rate
Both kill: the OOM killer handles CPU overuse as well
explain: CPU is compressible, so the kernel can withhold it and let the workload continue more slowly. Memory is not: once reclaim fails there is nothing left to withhold, so the cgroup's OOM killer runs and memory.events records the oom_kill. memory.high is the one memory knob that throttles rather than killing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
question: Which product is the best fit for explicit slot-based state tracking rather than pure query rewriting?
options: A job search with filters for role, level, location, remote and salary
An open-domain assistant answering follow-up questions about history
A chatbot that summarizes a single uploaded PDF
A spell checker
explain: Slot-based tracking needs a schema of constraints. The job search has one, which puts it on the task-oriented side of the line the CIS survey draws. Open-domain QA has no fixed schema and usually relies on rewriting.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
question: Your app stores only the chat transcript and re-derives state each turn. A user removes the remote filter by clicking its chip, then types *show staff roles too*. What is the likely bug?
options: The click is lost: the re-derived state brings remote back because the transcript still says only remote ones
The query builder crashes on a missing slot
Joint goal accuracy cannot be computed
There is no bug; re-derivation handles UI edits automatically
explain: UI edits are not in the transcript unless you write them there. Re-deriving from text alone resurrects the removed filter. Either log UI events into the history or keep server-side state that the click updates directly.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
question: Why does comparing the two orders of a question reveal unfaithfulness that reading each CoT alone would miss?
options: Because the judge model can only read short CoTs
Because each CoT can be locally valid, while the pair shows that something unstated, here the order of the names, changed the answer
Because reversed questions always have the answer Yes
Because the model refuses one of the two orders
explain: Every individual argument in the river example is plausible. Only the pair exposes that the standard of reasoning changed with the order, which the CoT never mentions. That is the counterfactual test of lesson 1, with the change made by the question's wording instead of a planted cue.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
question: In the naive loop, the kernel launch itself returns immediately. Why does the batch still take 61 ms?
options: Kernel launches are only asynchronous when a stream is given explicitly
cudaMemcpy always runs on a separate thread, which serializes with the launch
The SMs cannot accept a kernel while a copy engine is active
The D2H cudaMemcpy is in the same stream as the kernel and blocks the host until the kernel and the copy both finish
explain: A launch with no stream argument goes into the legacy default stream and returns at once. The very next statement is a blocking cudaMemcpy in that same stream, so it cannot start until the kernel finishes, and it does not return to the host until the copy finishes. The host is pinned to the GPU's pace.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Two kernels at once: concurrency, stream priorities, comm overlap
question: A 216-block decode kernel (two full waves on 108 SMs, one block per SM) is running. 0.10 ms later you launch a 20-block kernel on a second stream of equal priority. In the toy model, when does the small kernel start?
options: At 0.10 ms, because separate streams always run concurrently
At 1.00 ms, as soon as the first wave frees SMs
At 2.00 ms: every SM is busy, and when wave 1 ends the big kernel's waiting blocks were queued first
Never, because two kernels cannot share a GPU
explain: Streams only permit overlap. With every SM occupied there is no room, and the dispatcher serves the earlier-launched kernel's remaining 108 blocks first when wave 1 finishes. The small kernel gets SMs only at 2.00 ms and ends at 2.25 ms, exactly as if it were on the same stream.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: In an inference server: double buffering and reading the gaps
question: Why does double buffering need two pinned buffers rather than one, if the copy is asynchronous anyway?
options: Because the host would otherwise overwrite bytes the copy engine is still reading, so it must wait for the copy to finish before preparing the next chunk
A single pinned buffer cannot be larger than one page-locked allocation
Because each CUDA stream requires its own pinned allocation
Because cudaMemcpyAsync needs a separate destination buffer per call
explain: Asynchrony means the host returns early, not that the buffer is free. With one buffer the host must wait until the engine has finished reading it, which rebuilds the serial schedule. A second buffer lets the host fill B while the engine drains A; an event records when A is released.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The LLM engine loop: hiding CPU scheduling behind the GPU
question: On a lightly loaded vLLM v0.6 server you raise --num-scheduler-steps from 1 to 10. What should you expect?
options: Lower time to first token, because scheduling happens less often
Possibly better throughput, but new requests wait for the current 10 steps, so time to first token rises at low load and tokens arrive in bursts
No change, since multi-step only matters for prefill
The GPU idles more, because it must wait for ten schedules
explain: Multi-step scheduling spreads one scheduling pass over n steps, which reduces CPU overhead per step. vLLM's post lists the trade-offs: bumpy inter-token latency, since output tokens for several steps are returned together, and higher time to first token (TTFT) at low request rates, since a new request can start only after the current multi-step run finishes.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: A reranker trained with random negatives scores 0.95 on a held-out set of (positive, random negative) pairs but barely beats BM25 when deployed behind a strong dense retriever. What is the most likely cause?
options: The training negatives were easy, so the model never learned to separate the plausible near-misses it sees in deployment
The learning rate was too low
Sigmoid outputs should have been used instead of logits
max_length was set to 512 instead of 1,024
explain: This is the failure LCE addresses. Random negatives are separable by surface cues, so the evaluation looks great while the deployed candidate lists contain only plausible passages. Mine negatives from the target retriever's top results.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes, hex and XOR: the alphabet of cryptography
question: What is 17 mod 5?
explain: 17 = 3 x 5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Modes of operation: why ECB leaks and what CBC and CTR fix
question: In CTR mode, what must never repeat under the same key?
options: The plaintext
The ciphertext length
The padding
The counter block (nonce and counter)
explain: A repeated counter block repeats the keystream, which is the two-time pad from lesson 4. SP 800-38A requires every counter block under a key to be unique, across all messages.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
question: A webhook handler checks `if request_sig == expected_sig:`. What is the risk, and the fix?
options: No risk; both are strings
Length extension; switch to MD5
Replay; switch to Base64
Timing side channel; compare with hmac.compare_digest
explain: String == exits at the first mismatch, leaking how many leading bytes match through response time. hmac.compare_digest compares in time that does not depend on the content.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding
question: What does an attacker actually need to compute the private exponent d from the public key (n, e)?
options: Nothing more: d can be computed from e alone
The ciphertext c = 2790
A larger public exponent e
The prime factors p and q of n, because phi = (p-1)(q-1) needs them
explain: phi needs the factors of n, and d is the inverse of e mod phi. For n = 3233 the factors 61 and 53 are found instantly, so the toy key is broken; factoring a 3072-bit n is believed infeasible, and that is RSA's whole security.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Unauthenticated encryption: why decryption must refuse first
question: Why is encrypt-then-MAC the safe order for combining a cipher with a MAC?
options: The MAC hides the plaintext length
It is faster because the MAC runs on shorter data
It lets the receiver skip the MAC when the padding is valid
The receiver verifies the tag on the received bytes before any decryption or padding code runs
explain: With encrypt-then-MAC the tag covers the ciphertext and IV, so forgeries are rejected before decryption, and padding errors can never be observed for data the sender did not create. It does not hide length, and the MAC must always be checked.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Fixed IVs in homemade protocols: Zerologon
question: Which change in Microsoft's fix also removed a downgrade route?
options: Requiring secure RPC (signing and sealing) instead of letting clients negotiate it
Switching from AES to Triple DES
Lengthening the machine account password
Moving Netlogon to a new port
explain: Optional protection lets an attacker simply not ask for it. Making signing and sealing mandatory removed that choice; the enforcement phase in February 2021 extended it to all devices.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Never trust parameters: invalid curves, blank signatures, pinning
question: Your service receives P-256 public keys from clients as raw (x, y) integers and builds them with `ec.EllipticCurvePublicNumbers(x, y, ec.SECP256R1())`. The library documentation warns this object is not validated until `.public_key()` is called. What should the code do?
options: Call .public_key() (which validates the point) and reject on error before any key agreement
Use the numbers directly in the multiplication for speed
Check only that x and y are less than 2^256
Hash the point before using it
explain: The cryptography documentation says EllipticCurvePublicNumbers is not validated until public_key() succeeds. A range check alone does not test the curve equation or subgroup; SP 800-56A's full validation needs all four checks.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
question: What index does the layout (2,(2,2)):(4,(2,1)) give for the 2-D coordinate (1,2)?
explain: The column coordinate 2 splits in the nested shape (2,2) as (0,1). The natural coordinate is (1,(0,1)), so the index is 1 x 4 + 0 x 2 + 1 x 1 = 5. The CuTe docs print this layout as rows 0 2 1 3 and 4 6 5 7.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
question: A model has M = 512, N = 512, K = 16384 GEMMs, and a 128x128 tile kernel launches only 16 CTAs on a 132-SM GPU. Which CUTLASS technique targets this case most directly?
options: Ping-Pong schedule
Split-K or Stream-K across the K dimension
More pipeline stages
A larger 256x128 tile
explain: With only 16 output tiles, most SMs idle no matter how each CTA is pipelined. Splitting K (split-K or stream-K) creates more parallel work and reduces the partial sums. A larger tile makes even fewer CTAs.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
question: A region is 2-way interleaved with 1024-byte granularity. Which device and DPA offset hold host offset 3500?
options: Device 1, DPA 428
Device 0, DPA 1452
Device 0, DPA 3500
Device 1, DPA 1452
explain: 3500 / 1024 rounded down = chunk 3; 3 mod 2 = 1, so device 1. Rounds before it: 3 / 2 rounded down = 1, so DPA = 1 x 1024 + (3500 mod 1024) = 1024 + 428 = 1452.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The CFAA: access, authorisation, damage and loss
question: An insider uses their own valid login to copy files they are allowed to read, then sells them. Which CFAA phrase is the main legal question?
options: Whether they 'exceeded authorized access'
Whether the files caused 'damage'
Whether the act was 'extortion' under (a)(7)
Whether the computer was 'protected'
explain: The login was valid, so 'without authorization' is unlikely; the question is whether obtaining those files exceeded authorised access. That is exactly the question Van Buren answered in 2021, next lesson.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
question: A security tool has many legitimate uses. Under Article 6, what generally has to be shown for its distribution to be a Convention offence?
options: Only that it could be misused by someone
That it was distributed for free
That it was written in a European country
That it was designed or adapted primarily for committing offences, and distributed with intent that it be used for them
explain: Article 6 deliberately avoids criminalising dual-use tools: it requires the 'designed or adapted primarily' test plus intent, and excludes authorised testing and protection. Lesson 7 shows how national laws apply the same idea.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
question: Under the US Wiretap Act, which exception most directly lets a company's security team inspect traffic on its own email service to protect the service?
options: The provider exception for protecting the rights or property of the provider
The computer trespasser exception
Section 1201 of the DMCA
There is no exception; all inspection is illegal
explain: 2511(2)(a)(i) covers employees or agents of a communication service provider intercepting in the normal course of employment as a necessary incident to the service or to protect the provider's rights or property. The trespasser exception is for people acting under colour of law.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
question: A stranger finds an exposed database of customer records through a search engine for internet-exposed services. Which action best follows the checklist?
options: Download a full copy to prove the scale
Report privately to the owner (or a national CERT) what is visible, without logging in or keeping data
Post the address publicly so the owner is forced to act
Log in once to check whether the data is real
explain: No authority means no access beyond what is openly visible. Minimal data, private reporting and keeping nothing protect both the people in the database and the finder.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
question: A reviewer says: 'DoReMi just upweights web text, so it must trade away academic domains.' Which result refutes this most directly?
options: Pile-CC's weight rose to 0.6057
The 8B DoReMi model has lower log-perplexity than the baseline on all 22 domains, including ArXiv and PubMed Central
The proxy model cost only 8% of the main model's FLOPs
explain: The claim is about a tradeoff on academic domains. Table 4 shows held-out perplexity improved on every domain, including the most heavily downweighted ones.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
question: Why test a new 5B-token dataset with a short anneal from a half-trained checkpoint instead of a full pretraining run that includes it?
options: Anneals are the only way to measure benchmark scores
Full runs cannot include datasets smaller than 10B tokens
A full run would repeat the dataset too often
The anneal costs a few percent of a full run, and the decay phase is where a small, high-quality source shows its effect
explain: Llama 3 anneals an 8B checkpoint over 40B tokens with 30 percent new data; OLMo 2's microanneals were even smaller. Both rely on the decay phase being where data changes show up, at a small fraction of the compute of a scaling study or a full run. Repetition is not the issue: the anneal's 30 percent of 40B reads 5B tokens over twice.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
question: A 64-byte AoS record has 16 four-byte fields. A loop streams 10 million records and reads 2 fields. What does the model predict for AoS vs SoA traffic?
options: Equal: both read 10 million records
AoS reads 640 MB, SoA reads 80 MB, an 8x difference
AoS reads 640 MB, SoA reads 320 MB, a 2x difference
SoA reads more because it opens 2 separate streams
explain: AoS: 10,000,000 x 64 bytes = 640 MB. SoA: 10,000,000 x 8 bytes (two 4-byte fields) = 80 MB. The ratio is $S/k = 64/8 = 8$. Two streams is no problem for a sequential scan; the touched bytes are all useful.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
question: A loop checks `if (e.is_burning)` on 100,000 entities every frame, and about 1% are burning. Following existential processing, what change helps most?
options: Pack is_burning into a bit field inside the entity struct
Keep a separate table of burning entities and run the loop only over it
Sort entities so burning ones come first, but keep the flag check
Move is_burning to the start of the struct
explain: With a burning table, row existence is the boolean. The loop touches about 1,000 rows instead of streaming the cache lines of all 100,000 entities just to read a flag that is almost always false.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
question: A deletion job meets a record that is under a legal hold and past its retention date. What should it do?
options: Delete it, because retention dates are mandatory
Skip it and log that it was skipped because of the hold
Anonymise it instead
Ask the user
explain: Holds override deletion until legal releases them (Purview's 'retention wins over deletion'). Deleting held records can be a serious legal problem; changing them by anonymising is also a change. The job should skip and record why, so the record is deleted once the hold ends.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security II: auditing reads and the Snowflake thefts
question: Why could a rule that alerts only on failed logins and permission errors miss the Snowflake thefts entirely?
options: The intruders used valid credentials and ran commands their accounts were allowed to run, so nothing failed
Snowflake does not log failed logins
The intruders deleted the audit logs
Temporary stages hide queries from the query history
explain: Every step used a valid password and permitted commands, so there were no failures to alert on. The query history still recorded each statement; the temporary stage disappears at session end, but the COPY and GET statements remain in history.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Media sanitisation: clear, purge and destroy (NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2)
question: A laptop SSD was encrypted with full disk encryption from the day it was issued. Under SP 800-88 Rev. 2, what is a fast purge option before reissuing it?
options: Run a single-file shredder on sensitive folders
Degauss the drive
Delete the user profile
Cryptographic erase: sanitise the encryption key, provided no copy of it survives elsewhere
explain: Because nothing was ever stored in plaintext, sanitising every copy of the key purges the data. Shredders fail on SSDs (Wei et al.), degaussing does not work on flash, and deleting a profile only removes pointers.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeypots by interaction: low, medium and high
question: You want to know the moment anyone on your internal network tries to log in to a fake database server. Which honeypot fits best?
options: A high-interaction database server with real data, so the intruder stays longer
A network telescope on the Internet
A low-interaction decoy that answers the database port and logs every connection and login attempt
A medium-interaction shell honeypot exposed to the Internet
explain: Detection inside your network needs only the attempt, and a low-interaction decoy gives that at almost no risk. Real data in a decoy is a breach waiting to happen; Internet-facing decoys answer a different question.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Decoy cloud keys: the AWS key canary and the Grafana catch
question: Why does a decoy key with no permissions still produce a useful alert?
options: AWS emails the account owner whenever a powerless key is used
The secret key contains a tracking pixel
Keys without permissions are rejected before reaching AWS, which triggers an alarm
The attacker's very first test call, such as GetCallerIdentity, needs no permissions and is recorded in CloudTrail
explain: The attacker must use the key to learn what it opens. GetCallerIdentity works for any valid key and is logged, so the attempt itself is the signal.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Alert fidelity: false triggers, fingerprinting and upkeep
question: Vetterl and Clayton could spot thousands of honeypots with one packet. What made that possible?
options: The honeypots used off-the-shelf protocol libraries that behave slightly differently from the real servers they imitate
Every honeypot had the word honeypot in its banner
Honeypots always run on port 2222
The honeypots were listed in a public directory
explain: Protocol implementation differences are a structural giveaway, which is why the authors called it a class break. Changing banners alone does not fix it.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Batch-dependent numerics and the token that flips
question: A server at temperature 0 returns different text for the same prompt under load, even though every kernel is run-to-run deterministic. What is the mechanism?
options: Temperature 0 still draws from the RNG, so the seed matters after all.
The KV cache quantizes older entries when memory gets tight.
The scheduler truncates long prompts differently under load.
Load changes the batch size and your position in it, which changes the reduction shape inside the kernels and perturbs your logits.
explain: Run-to-run determinism says a fixed launch gives fixed bits. Under load the launch is not fixed: batch size and position change the split count, the tile and sometimes the kernel. The logits move by a few last bits, and a greedy argmax at a near-tie turns that into a different token.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
question: A cached and an uncached run emit different token ids but detokenize to the same text. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The cache is broken and the test should fail.
The test should only ever compare at the text level, since text is what users receive.
Users are unaffected, but the numerics genuinely differ, so a logit-level or bitwise test is the one that will localize the cause.
The tokenizer is nondeterministic and should be reseeded.
explain: Identical text with different ids is possible, so text equality is the weakest of the three levels. It is the right contract to promise a user and the wrong instrument for finding the cause, which lives in the logits. Compare at the logit level to localize, then state the guarantee at the level you actually promise.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
question: Using FoundationDB's defaults, what is the probability that two specific buggify sites are *both* activated in the same run?
explain: Each site is activated independently with probability 0.25 once per run, so both are active with $0.25 \times 0.25 = 0.0625$, about 1 run in 16. Rare pairs still happen often across tens of thousands of runs per night.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
question: A team stores the pipeline definition in a separate repository that only the platform team can edit. The pipeline runs `npm test` on every developer branch with a registry token in the environment. Are they safe from PPE?
options: No: this is the indirect form. Anyone who can push a branch can change package.json scripts or test files that npm test runs
Yes, because the CI file cannot be edited by developers
Yes, as long as the token is masked in logs
No, but only if the repository is public
explain: OWASP lists exactly this as I-PPE: the CI config is protected, but files it executes are not. Masking only hides values in logs; code that runs can still send the token anywhere.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: OIDC from CI, precisely: subject claims and environments
question: A team's apply role trusts `StringLike` `repo:acme/infra:ref:refs/heads/*`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: it pins the repository
It accepts tokens from other organisations
StringLike cannot be used with OIDC
It accepts tokens from every branch, so a pushed feature branch can assume the apply role
explain: The * matches any branch name. Trust the environment subject exactly, and let the environment's branch rule decide which branch may deploy.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Scanners in the pipeline: Checkov, Trivy and zizmor
question: Checkov passes a workflow that uses pull_request_target and checks out the PR head commit, while zizmor fails it. What is the right conclusion?
options: Checkov is broken and should be removed
The workflow is safe because one scanner passed it
Tools have different rule sets; run a workflow-specific analyser alongside a general IaC scanner, and treat a pass as "no known pattern found", not "safe"
zizmor is wrong, because pull_request_target is required for forks
explain: In the real run only zizmor's dangerous-triggers audit flagged the pwn request. A clean scan only means no rule matched.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
question: In the finished pipeline, why do pull requests get a separate read-only plan role instead of the apply role?
options: PR code is untrusted and plan can run provider or PR-controlled code; a read-only role means that code cannot change the cloud even if it runs
Read-only roles are faster
The apply role cannot run terraform plan
GitHub forbids write roles on pull requests
explain: Lessons 2 and 9: anything that runs during a PR may be attacker-controlled. Giving it only read access caps the damage, while reviewers still see a real plan.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
question: Why does training on t drawn from all of [0, 1] matter for generation, compared with BERT's fixed 15%?
options: Generation starts from a fully masked sequence, so the model must be good at predicting with almost no context; a fixed 15% ratio never trains that regime
Uniform t makes training cheaper per step
It lets the model use a causal mask
It removes the need for a tokenizer
explain: Sampling walks t from 1 down to 0, visiting every masking ratio. A model that only ever saw 15% masks has never learned the early, nearly empty steps, and its loss is not a likelihood bound.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
question: A team runs DPO on a diffusion LM and estimates each of the four ELBOs (policy and reference, chosen and rejected) with its own fresh random masks. Training is unstable. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Switch to a causal attention mask during DPO
Lower the learning rate until the noise averages out
Estimate each ELBO with a single timestep and many masks at that timestep
Use the same timesteps and masks for the policy and reference estimates of each answer
explain: Antithetic sampling costs nothing extra: the policy and reference ELBOs share their randomness, so their errors cancel in the log-ratio that DPO uses. Spending a budget on one timestep with many masks is worse than spreading it over timesteps, and a smaller step size only slows learning.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
question: A team streams KV layer by layer, so per-request exposed transfer is only 10 ms. At peak, prefill GPUs produce 40 GB/s of KV, and the shared link carries 25 GB/s. What happens?
options: TTFT rises slightly but TPOT is unaffected
Decode GPUs simply run larger batches
Nothing, because overlap already hid the transfer
Transfers queue up without bound: the link cannot sustain the KV production rate, so decode starts slip further and prefill memory fills
explain: Overlap hides one transfer behind compute, but sustained bandwidth must still exceed rate x KV bytes. At 40 GB/s produced against 25 GB/s carried, the backlog grows. DistServe's 90 Gbps example is exactly this throughput check.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: What storage remembers: the BTK floppy disk (2005)
question: An examiner has recovered the deleted files and now asks: does data showing use by "Dennis" on a church computer identify the sender, and how strongly? Which NIST SP 800-86 phase is this?
options: Analysis
Collection
Examination
Reporting
explain: Recovering the files and their metadata was examination. Weighing what the facts mean for the question being asked is analysis. Reporting comes after, when the conclusion and its limits are written down.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Eight NTFS timestamps, and how timestomping gets caught
question: Why is last-access time weak evidence on NTFS?
options: It is stored only in FN, which users cannot see
Updates to it can be deferred by up to an hour and can be disabled entirely
It uses local time instead of UTC
It records the time the antivirus scanned the file
explain: Microsoft documents that NTFS may defer last-access updates by up to one hour and that the update can be turned off (disablelastaccess). It is a FILETIME in UTC and exists in SI too.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
question: Why does carving deleted files from a Windows 11 laptop's NVMe SSD usually fail?
options: NVMe drives do not use sectors
With delete notifications (TRIM) on by default, the drive is told freed blocks are unused and typically clears them
Windows 11 encrypts deleted files with a separate key
Carving only works on FAT
explain: Delete notification tells the drive which clusters were freed, and the drive's garbage collection makes them read back empty. CyBOK cites near-zero recovery on TRIM-aware systems. Carving is file system independent, and NVMe still exposes blocks.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Mobile forensics: extraction levels, encryption and isolation
question: Why does NIST caution that logical extraction may modify data?
options: The connection type and protocol used to talk to the phone can change data on it, for example marking unread SMS as read
Logical extraction always wipes the phone
Logical extraction writes a forensic agent into the bootloader
It uses JTAG, which resets memory
explain: SP 800-101r1 notes that different connection methods and protocols may modify data, giving unread SMS as the example. It does not wipe the phone, and JTAG is level 3, not logical.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence law and writing the expert report
question: Your analysis shows a USB stick with VSN 1234-ABCD was mounted and a document on it was opened from the profile of user jsmith. Which sentence belongs in the opinion section?
options: J. Smith stole the payroll file
The jsmith profile opened payroll_export.csv from a removable volume with serial 1234-ABCD; this is consistent with, but does not by itself establish, J. Smith personally doing so
The USB stick belongs to J. Smith
No conclusions can be drawn from artefacts
explain: The opinion should state what the artefacts support (an account and a volume) and its limits. Attributing the act to a person or ownership of the stick needs other evidence; saying nothing ignores real findings.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds
question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: Why can DPO ignore the partition function $Z(x)$, which sums over every possible response?
options: It is always equal to 1 for a normalized language model
It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the reward difference that Bradley-Terry uses
DPO estimates it with Monte Carlo samples from the policy
It is absorbed into the learning rate
explain: $\beta \log Z(x)$ is the same for every answer to a given prompt. Bradley-Terry compares two answers to the same prompt through $r(y_w) - r(y_l)$, so the term cancels exactly. No sampling or approximation is needed.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: You train with cDPO at $\epsilon = 0.1$, $\beta = 0.1$, and a pair already has margin 3. What does its gradient do?
options: It pushes the margin back down toward ln 9, about 2.2
Nothing: the loss is already near 0
It keeps widening the margin, but more slowly than DPO
It flips the label of that pair
explain: cDPO's weight is $(1-\epsilon) - \sigma(m) = 0.9 - 0.9526 = -0.0526$: negative, so the update shrinks the gap toward the target where $\sigma(m) = 0.9$. Plain DPO's weight there would be 0.0474, still widening. rDPO would push harder still.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
question: Why can a policy that puts 90% on a never-labeled answer still minimize the DPO loss in Xu et al.'s example?
options: Because the DPO loss depends only on the probabilities of the labeled answers, so unlabeled ones are unconstrained
Because beta is too small
Because the reference model is wrong
Because DPO adds a length penalty
explain: With one pair, the loss depends only on $\pi(y_1)$ and $\pi(y_2)$; it is minimized once $\pi(y_2) = 0$, wherever the rest of the mass goes. PPO's optimum multiplies by the reference probability, which is 0 for $y_3$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
question: The candidate block raises an exception on 2 percent of reads during the experiment. What do users see?
options: Errors on 2 percent of requests
Errors only when the experiment is enabled
The normal control result; the exceptions are recorded as mismatches for engineers
A retry against the old store after a delay
explain: Scientist swallows and records exceptions raised in the try block and returns the control value. The README does warn that it does not protect against candidate timeouts, so slow candidates can still hurt users.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH's fine print: signed prekeys, replay, deniability, misbinding
question: Why is the prekey signature needed, given that DH1 and DH2 already authenticate both parties?
options: To make the message deniable
Because X25519 keys cannot be used without signatures
To let Bob prove to a judge that Alice wrote the message
So a malicious server cannot plant its own prekey and later unlock the session by stealing Bob's identity key
explain: That is the weak forward secrecy attack in section 4.5 of the spec. Signatures do not help deniability (the opposite), X25519 works fine unsigned, and X3DH deliberately avoids transcripts that prove authorship.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Lost and late messages: skipped keys, limits and header encryption
question: What does header encryption add to the Double Ratchet?
options: Hides ratchet public keys and message numbers from observers, so messages are harder to link and count
Forward secrecy for message bodies
Post-quantum security
Protection against device compromise
explain: Bodies already have FS and PCS. Encrypted headers stop an eavesdropper from reading the ratchet keys and counters that otherwise link messages into a session.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Metadata: sealed sender and the statistics that undo it
question: Which change would most directly weaken the statistical disclosure attack described here?
options: Delaying, batching or padding automatic receipts so they stop marking a tight time window
Longer safety numbers
Using AES-256 instead of AES-128
Rotating the signed prekey weekly
explain: The attack lives on timing. Breaking the tight link between delivery and reply (or adopting the paper's provably secure protocol changes) is what helps; stronger ciphers and key rotation do not touch metadata.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Many devices per person: Sesame, fan-out and linked-device phishing
question: In Sesame's model, who holds the authoritative list of a user's devices?
options: Each contact's phone
A blockchain
The user's SIM card
The server, which senders consult before fanning out
explain: Sesame assumes a server that stores the current record of users and devices. That makes device-list changes a server-side power unless clients authenticate them: WhatsApp has the primary phone sign the device list, and Automatic Device Verification and security codes cover all devices, so the server cannot silently add one.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Operational failures: Signalgate and the TeleMessage archive (2025)
question: You use real Signal; your contact uses TM SGNL. Where can your messages to them end up in plaintext?
options: Nowhere; your app encrypts end to end
On TeleMessage's archive server, because the contact's modified client copies decrypted messages there
On Signal's servers
In your own backup only
explain: Encryption ends at the recipient's device, and that device's client forwarded plaintext to an archive. Micah Lee also notes Signal users cannot tell when a contact runs TM SGNL.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: In a kretprobe on a function, you try to print arg0 to see which file descriptor was passed in. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Arguments are not available at return in a kretprobe; save them in a map keyed by tid at entry, or use fexit, which still has args
Nothing; arg0 is preserved for kretprobe
kretprobes cannot access any data at all; use printf instead
You must cast arg0 to a pointer first
explain: A kretprobe only has retval: argument registers may have been overwritten by the time the function returns. Save what you need at entry, keyed by tid, or use fexit, whose args remain available on return.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A colleague's kprobe-based script worked last year but now fails to attach after a kernel upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: The verifier became stricter about printf
bpftrace no longer supports kprobes
Tracepoints replaced all kprobes
The probed kernel function was renamed, removed or changed, because kprobes target internal, unstable functions
explain: kprobes can attach to almost any kernel function, but those functions are not an API. Tracepoints, or fentry with BTF types, are more resilient. By default bpftrace exits with an error if any probe fails to attach, unless the missing_probes config is set to warn or ignore.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: Why do the gradients in QAT use the straight-through estimator instead of the true derivative of round()?
options: The true derivative is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient would reach the weights
round() is not implemented on GPUs
The estimator makes training faster but changes the final model format
It removes the need for calibration
explain: round() is a step function: its derivative is zero except at the jumps, where it is undefined. Treating the quantizer as identity inside the clipping range lets gradients flow so the float weights can move to positions that quantize well.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
question: In the toy server, why is '/assets/html5/../../../../data/sessions.db' served by the vulnerable check?
options: Python's normpath has a bug
The file is inside the web root
The rule tests the raw text for an allowed folder name, and only resolves the path after deciding
The '..' characters are removed automatically
explain: The decision is made on the text, which contains OPEN_DIR, so the '..' refusal is skipped. The fixed version decides on the resolved location, which is outside the root.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Exposure management: what you show the internet, continuously
question: Your external scan finds a NetScaler Gateway on an address that is not in the inventory. What should happen first?
options: Ignore it until a vulnerability scanner flags a CVE
Treat it as a finding now: find the owner, confirm the version and support status, and block it if no owner appears
Run an exploit against it to prove it is vulnerable
Delete it from the scan results
explain: An unowned internet-facing edge product is a risk before any CVE is known: nobody patches it or reads its logs. Testing it with an exploit is out of bounds unless you own it and have authorisation; ownership comes first.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
question: A Cisco firewall's core dump analysis returns 'Compromise Detected'. Under ED 25-03, what should you do with the device first?
options: Disconnect it from the network but keep it powered on, report it and work on eviction
Reboot it to clear the malware
Install the patch and put it back in service
Power it off immediately
explain: Disconnecting stops the intruder using it; keeping power preserves memory for analysis. A reboot does not remove this malware (the directive later required a full power removal as part of remediation, after evidence collection).

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
question: During a GRPO run, reward has been flat for 200 steps while mean response length keeps rising. Split by outcome, correct responses hold at about 1,500 tokens and incorrect ones grow from 3,000 to 7,000. What should you change first?
options: Add a large constant penalty per token so every response shrinks
Lower the temperature so the model explores less
Train longer: length growth means the model is learning to think more deeply
Replace per-response length normalization in the loss with a constant normalizer (Dr. GRPO), then re-check the two length curves
explain: Growth confined to wrong answers with no reward gain is the signature of the loss bias: wrong answers are penalized less per token as they lengthen. Fix the normalizer first. A blanket length penalty would also shorten the correct answers, which are not the problem.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
question: A product needs answers under 1,500 output tokens from a reasoning model. Responses often come back incomplete with no visible text. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The model is refusing; rephrase the prompt
The output cap is cutting off hidden reasoning; lower the effort level (or thinking budget) and leave headroom in the cap
Temperature is too high; set it to 0
The cap counts only visible tokens, so raise it to the context length
explain: Reasoning tokens count toward the output limit. If the model plans a long think, a tight cap truncates it before the answer. Lowering effort changes the plan; the cap only stops it.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Double decoding and path normalisation
question: Why is checking `".." in path` on the raw request weaker than resolving the path and checking where it lands?
options: Because `in` is slow on long strings
Because `..` is legal in file names
Because Python strings are immutable
Because the filesystem, not the string check, decides what `..`, separators and links finally mean
explain: Encodings, backslashes on Windows, repeated slashes and symbolic links all change where a path lands. Resolving first and checking the resolved location makes the decision on the same meaning the filesystem will use.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Canonical identifiers and idempotence: the Spotify takeover
question: RFC 8264 says to reapply PRECIS rules until the output is stable. What should happen if it is still changing after three extra rounds?
options: Reject the input string as invalid
Fall back to ASCII lower-casing
Use the last output anyway
Keep applying the rules until it stops
explain: The RFC says the implementation "SHOULD terminate application of the rules and reject the input string as invalid". Looping forever would be a denial-of-service risk, and accepting an unstable value recreates the Spotify bug.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Bidirectional text and Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574)
question: Which statement about directional isolates (U+2066 to U+2069) is correct according to UAX #9?
options: Text inside an isolate does not affect the ordering of text outside it, and vice versa
They were part of Unicode 1.0
They are always ignored by renderers
They are safe to allow anywhere in source code
explain: UAX #9 introduced isolates in Unicode 6.3 because embeddings affected their surroundings too strongly. They are still invisible reordering controls, so Rust's lints reject them in comments and literals along with embeddings and overrides.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Polyglot files, content sniffing and LangSec
question: Which practice best follows the LangSec idea of recognising the whole input before acting on it?
options: Process each field as soon as it is read, to save memory
Accept malformed input and repair it, as Postel's law suggests
Use regular expressions to block known-bad substrings
Parse and validate the entire input against a strict grammar, and only then act on it
explain: Acting on partial input means the system may have done something before it discovers the input was invalid. Repairing input and blocklisting substrings both widen the accepted language instead of fixing it.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
question: A manifest-based provider is already enabled into three sessions. Can an EDR sensor enable it into a fourth?
options: No, each provider serves exactly one session
Only if the first three are stopped
Yes, manifest-based and TraceLogging providers can be enabled by up to eight sessions
Only for MOF providers
explain: Microsoft's documentation states manifest-based and TraceLogging providers can be enabled by up to eight trace sessions simultaneously; the older MOF and WPP types only by one at a time.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Process injection as telemetry: Sysmon events 8, 10 and 25
question: Sysmon event 8 shows a remote thread created in explorer.exe with StartModule and StartFunction empty. Why does that matter?
options: Sysmon could not map the thread's start address to any loaded module or export, which is typical of code placed in memory with no file behind it
It means Sysmon is misconfigured
It proves the thread belongs to Windows Update
Empty fields mean the thread failed to start
explain: Sysmon infers StartModule and StartFunction and documents that they may be empty when the start address lies outside loaded modules or known exports. Legitimate remote threads usually start in a known module function.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Attack surface reduction rules: blocking risky behaviours
question: An admin runs `Set-MpPreference` with one GUID and action Enabled to turn on a single new rule. What happens to the five rules configured earlier on that machine?
options: They are replaced: Set-MpPreference overwrites the existing rule list with the values given
They stay as they were
They switch to Audit
They switch to Warn
explain: Microsoft documents that Set-MpPreference overwrites existing ASR rules and modes; Add-MpPreference appends without affecting existing values. A one-line Set can silently disable protections.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: What kernel sensors cost: CrowdStrike Channel File 291 (July 2024)
question: Which change would most directly have limited how many machines crashed, even with the bug present?
options: Staggered deployment of Rapid Response Content starting with a canary group
A faster SIEM
Longer passwords
Disabling ETW
explain: A canary rollout exposes the update to a small set of hosts first; a crash there stops the rollout before it reaches the whole sensor base. CrowdStrike adopted this for Rapid Response Content after the incident.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
question: A house has 10 appliances with 3 states each. How many joint states does the equivalent single HMM have?
explain: Joint states are K to the power N = 3^10 = 59,049. 30 would be K times N (independent chains, which is what approximate methods exploit), 1,000 is 10^3 with base and exponent swapped, and 3,628,800 is 10 factorial.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match
question: You block company records on the first 3 letters of the raw (uncleaned) name. Which true duplicate pair is most likely to be lost?
options: `Quantix, Inc.` and `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc`
`Quantix, Inc.` and `Quantix Inc`
`Brightline Labs LLC` and `Brightline Labs, Inc.`
explain: Full-width letters are different code points, so the raw prefixes differ even though the text looks identical. The other two pairs share the raw prefix `Qua` or `Bri`. Blocking keys must be computed from cleaned values.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
question: In a rerun, old cluster X (40 records) and old cluster Y (3 records) merge into one cluster that contains all 43. Under the largest-overlap rule, what happens to the IDs?
options: Both IDs are deleted and a new one is minted
Y survives because it is the newer cluster
X survives; Y is kept as a redirect to X so links stored with Y still resolve
Both IDs survive and point to the same cluster forever, with no redirect needed
explain: The new cluster shares 40 records with X and 3 with Y, so X keeps its ID: the fewest stored references change. Y must not simply vanish, because profiles, saved searches and analytics tables may still hold it, so it becomes a redirect.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
question: Which grant should an investigator treat as the most dangerous in a review of consent grants?
options: User.Read delegated, consented by one user
Mail.ReadWrite as an application permission on a non-Microsoft app nobody recognises
openid and profile for a verified Microsoft app
Files.Read delegated, consented by one user
explain: Application permissions work without any user and cover the whole tenant, and write access lets the app change or send mail. Microsoft's playbook places app-only versions of the Mail permissions, and all write-capable app-only permissions, at the top of the review list.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
question: Storm-2372 obtained a PRT through a device it registered. Which response removes that foothold most directly?
options: Resetting the user's password only
Disabling or deleting the attacker-registered device in Entra ID and revoking the user's sessions
Enabling security defaults
Blocking the user's home IP address
explain: Microsoft lists disabling or deleting the device as invalidating its PRT. A password reset invalidates PRTs obtained with the password, but the device remains registered; revoking sessions clears the refresh tokens as well.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
question: After containing an Octo Tempest-style intrusion, which audit activity indicates persistence that survives resetting every compromised user?
options: User registered security info
Set domain authentication (a domain switched to federated)
Reset password (self-service)
Update user
explain: Federating a domain to an attacker's identity provider lets them sign tokens for any user in that domain, independent of user passwords. It must be found and reverted, and the federation settings of every domain reviewed.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: select and poll: readiness that costs O(n) per call
question: A proxy holds 50,000 mostly idle connections and wakes about 1,000 times per second. Which change cuts per-wakeup kernel work the most?
options: Switch from poll to select
Raise FD_SETSIZE to 65536 and keep select
Move to epoll so the kernel keeps the interest set and returns only ready descriptors
Call poll with a timeout of 0
explain: With poll every wakeup copies and scans 50,000 entries, so the scan repeats 1,000 times a second. epoll stores the interest set in the kernel once and each wait touches only ready items. select is worse (bitmap rebuilds, 1024 limit), and a zero timeout only turns waiting into spinning.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
question: A teammate tried 40 reranker configurations on a 50-query public set and reports the best one improved nDCG@10 by +0.035 over the baseline. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it, since +0.035 is larger than typical noise on 50 queries
Re-run the same 40 configurations on the same 50 queries with a different random seed to confirm
Score only the chosen configuration (and the baseline) once on a fresh query set that played no part in the choice
Report the average of all 40 configurations instead of the best one
explain: The +0.035 is a maximum over 40 noisy comparisons, so it is biased upward. In our toy, the best of 20 identical systems already gains about +0.038 on 50 queries from luck alone. Re-running on the same queries cannot remove that selection bias, and averaging all 40 answers a different question. A single evaluation on untouched queries gives an unbiased estimate.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
question: Which practice gives the strongest protection against both adaptive overfitting and contamination for a production search eval?
options: Averaging results over more public benchmarks
A private query set sampled from recent traffic, labeled in-house, read for a few pre-declared decisions and replaced on a schedule
Reporting results with five decimal places
Running the paired t-test with alpha = 0.01 instead of 0.05
explain: Recent private queries cannot be in a model's training data and have not been tuned against. Rotation keeps them from wearing out under repeated reads. More public benchmarks help external validity but stay exposed to contamination; stricter alpha alone does not address reuse.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
question: A non-PIE Linux executable runs with randomize_va_space set to 2. Which part of its memory is still at the same address on every run?
options: The main program's own code
The stack
The heap
Shared libraries such as libc
explain: Stack, heap and libraries are randomized. A non-PIE executable is linked for a fixed address, so its code stays put and remains a dependable source of reusable code. Building with -fPIE -pie lets the kernel move it too.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Memory tagging and hardened allocators against heap bugs
question: With random 4-bit MTE tags, a use-after-free happens to access memory that was re-tagged with the same value the stale pointer carries. What is the chance of this for one access, and what follows?
options: Zero: tags are never reused
1 in 16; the access is not detected, so MTE is probabilistic rather than a guarantee
1 in 256; the CPU detects it later
1 in 2; MTE only checks writes
explain: Four bits give 16 values. A random match goes undetected, which is why MTE is described as a strong probabilistic mitigation, and why allocators choose tags to differ from neighbours where they can.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
question: Which pair of mitigations, combined, covers both the return-address hijack and the function-pointer hijack of earlier lessons?
options: Stack canary and ASLR
A shadow stack (or PAC return signing) plus forward-edge CFI such as CFG or Clang CFI
NX and FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO and a sandbox
explain: Shadow stacks and PAC guard backward edges (returns); CFI, CFG, IBT and BTI guard forward edges (indirect calls and jumps). Canaries and ASLR only hinder, and NX and FORTIFY address different steps.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes
question: Eight threads update a shared histogram with 1,000,000 buckets of 8 bytes; updates land on random buckets. What is the best fix?
options: Give each thread a private histogram and merge them at the end
Pad every bucket to 64 bytes
Align the histogram array to 64 bytes
Use a bigger cache line size constant
explain: Padding every bucket would turn 8 MB into 64 MB and wreck cache use for little gain, since random buckets rarely collide. Per-thread histograms (fix 1) remove shared writes entirely, at the cost of 8 copies and one merge. Aligning the array only moves where the boundaries fall.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working
question: You halve B and keep E fixed. Which quantity changes the most?
options: Bytes uploaded per client per round, which doubles
SGD updates per client per round, which doubles
Rounds to the accuracy target, which always halves
The number of clients the server must wait for
explain: Updates per round are E times n_k over B, so halving B doubles them. Communication per round is set by the model size, not by B or E: one download and one upload of the parameters. Whether the extra local work converts into fewer rounds depends on how heterogeneous the clients are, so option C is exactly the trap.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: One model is not enough: personalization, async and vertical FL
question: Under Ditto with lambda = 1 on our toy, which client's personal model ends closest to its own local optimum?
options: Client A, because it holds the most data
All three move the same distance, since lambda is shared
Client C, because its steep local loss (a = 9) outweighs the penalty
Client B, because its optimum 2 is nearest to 2.3
explain: v_k = (a_k mu_k + lambda w*)/(a_k + lambda). At lambda = 1, C sits at 2.93, only 0.07 from its optimum 3, while A sits at 1.65, 0.65 from its optimum 1. Sample count does not enter the personal objective at all; curvature does.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Build it: a non-IID federated run in Flower, end to end
question: In one logged FedAvg run at alpha = 0.1, federated evaluation read 96.7 percent in round 16 and 89.3 percent in round 17, while centralized accuracy moved only from 94.1 to 93.9. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Federated evaluation is computed on the training data
The global model oscillates between rounds
Each round samples 10 different clients, whose held-out sets have very different label mixes and sizes, so the federated number is a noisy sample
Centralized evaluation is broken and should be ignored
explain: With highly skewed clients, how well the global model does depends on which digits a client holds. Sampling 10 of 50 clients per evaluation round makes the weighted average a noisy estimate; the 10000-image central test set is fixed. Look at both, and average federated metrics over several rounds.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN in production engines, and where it stops helping
question: Why did Weaviate, Lucene and Qdrant all ship ACORN-1 variants rather than ACORN-gamma?
options: ACORN-gamma reached lower recall than ACORN-1 in the paper
ACORN-gamma must know the predicates at build time
ACORN-1 removes the need for an exact fallback on restrictive filters
ACORN-1 runs on the HNSW graph already built: no gamma-times-larger lists and no rebuild, for more lookups per visited node
explain: ACORN-gamma is faster at search in the paper but builds 9x to 53x slower and stores longer lists; ACORN-1 works on existing graphs, which Weaviate cites directly (no reindexing). Both variants are predicate-agnostic, and every engine still keeps an exact scan for small match sets.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: Two teams report opposite results on shared experts: DeepSeekMoE finds them essential, OLMoE finds a shared expert slightly worse than an extra routed one. Which statement is best supported?
options: One of the two experiments must be wrong
Shared experts only help with softmax routers
It is open: the answer depends on granularity, combinations given up and balancing, and the 2.414 result measures a trained model's dependence, not a from-scratch comparison
Shared experts always help but cost more FLOPs
explain: Both are careful experiments with different designs. OLMoE compared two models trained from scratch at equal compute; DeepSeekMoE's from-scratch ablation was on a coarse GShard-style model, and its 2.414 number comes from disabling the expert after training. Later designs went both ways (V3 kept one; Qwen3 dropped them).

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Below the operating system: why boot code is the deepest foothold
question: An incident responder wipes a server's disks and reinstalls the OS, but the same backdoor reappears within minutes of the first boot. Which location best explains this?
options: A scheduled task in the new OS image
A browser extension synced from the cloud
An implant in the motherboard's SPI flash that rewrites the backdoor at boot
A malicious kernel module on the old disk
explain: Only the SPI flash survives a disk wipe and reinstall. A firmware implant such as LoJax (lesson 15) drops its payload into the fresh OS on every boot. The old disk is gone, and a fresh image has no scheduled task unless something wrote one.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: How firmware decides to run an image: db, dbx and the chain
