The kernel crashed back to bypass mode, where cgroups are ignored
cgroup CPU controls are passed to the BPF scheduler through callbacks and this scheduler does not implement them
explain: The kernel docs state the core reports cpu.max, cpu.weight and cpu.idle to the BPF scheduler via ops.cgroup_init() and cgroup_set_* callbacks, and each scheduler decides whether to implement them. Many ignore some of them, so read the scheduler's docs.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) and why deleting them fails
question: Which of these is the inbound variant of CWE-798?
options: A mobile app that ships with the API key for its backend
A CI job that reads a token from the CI secret store
A script that reads a database password from an environment variable
A router whose firmware accepts the same maintenance password on every unit
explain: Inbound means the product checks incoming logins against a credential built into it, identical everywhere. The mobile app is the outbound variant. The CI job and the environment-variable script keep the value out of the code, so they are not CWE-798, though they have their own risks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Splitting a key between people: Shamir's secret sharing
question: With a 3-of-5 split, how many shares can be lost or destroyed before the key becomes unrecoverable?
options: Any 2 can be lost; losing a third makes it unrecoverable
None
It is always recoverable from one share and the prime
explain: Recovery needs any 3 of the 5, so up to 2 may be lost. Choosing k and n trades availability (lower k, higher n) against the number of people an attacker must compromise (higher k).

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
question: Why does the root KSK use 3 of 7 Crypto Officers rather than 1 of 1 or 7 of 7?
options: 3 of 7 is required by FIPS 140-3
7 of 7 would be too slow for the HSM
Shamir's scheme only supports odd thresholds
1 of 1 lets one person misuse the key and 7 of 7 fails if anyone is ill; 3 of 7 needs collusion yet tolerates four absentees
explain: Threshold choice balances security (people needed to misuse) against availability (people who can be missing). FIPS 140-3 sets module requirements, not quorum sizes, and Shamir's scheme works for any k up to n.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
question: In a diff-based review, a new endpoint reads `request.headers['X-Account']` and passes it to a database query. Which question do you answer first?
options: Where the header value can come from and which sink it reaches
Whether the variable names follow the style guide
Whether the endpoint has unit tests for the happy path
Whether the query could be made faster with an index
explain: Headers are set by the client, so the value is a source an attacker controls, and a database query is a sink. Tracing source to sink comes first; style, speed and happy-path tests do not tell you whether a stranger can abuse it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
question: A team deploys with `--disable-proto=delete` and closes the ticket. Using the lodash case, what is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: without __proto__ there is no way to reach the prototype
constructor.prototype still reaches Object.prototype, as lodash's constructor payload did
The flag only affects browsers
The flag makes JSON.parse reject all objects
explain: --disable-proto removes the __proto__ accessor, but obj.constructor.prototype is another route to the same object. In our test the vulnerable merge was still polluted through it. Fix the merge itself.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
question: In the original goto fail code, why did the function report success after skipping the signature check?
options: The signature check returned success for every input
err still held 0 from the last successful hash update when control jumped to fail:
The compiler optimised the check away because of -O2
SSLFreeBuffer reset err to 0
explain: The jump happened right after a successful update, so err was 0, and fail: just returned it. The check itself was fine; it was never executed. The cleanup calls do not touch err.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
question: A crate exposes `pub fn get(&self, i: usize) -> &T { unsafe { self.items.get_unchecked(i) } }`. What is the review finding?
options: None: the code compiles, so the borrow checker proved it safe
The function is unsound: safe callers can pass any i and cause an out-of-bounds read
It should use a raw pointer instead of get_unchecked
It needs #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
explain: unsafe does not make the compiler check the precondition i < len; the programmer must. A public safe function that lets callers violate it is unsound. Check i < self.items.len() first, or simply use self.items[i]. forbid(unsafe_code) would reject the code rather than fix it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
question: Which recommendation is best for a path traversal finding in a download endpoint?
options: Reject names containing ../
Resolve the final path and refuse it unless it is inside the download folder; better, look files up by id; add a test with ../ and an absolute path
Log a warning when .. appears
Add a WAF rule for ../
explain: Blocking one spelling misses absolute paths and encodings, and logging or a WAF rule only detects. Checking the resolved path (or not taking paths from users at all) removes the class, and the test keeps it removed.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
question: A responder receives thousands of IKE_SA_INIT requests per second from spoofed source addresses. Which mechanism lets it avoid doing Diffie-Hellman work for them?
options: The anti-replay window on the Child SA
Traffic selectors in IKE_AUTH
Switching IKE to UDP port 4500
Returning a COOKIE notification and processing only requests that echo it back
explain: The cookie is computed from a responder secret and the initiator's address, so only an initiator that really receives packets at that address can echo it. The anti-replay window protects ESP data, traffic selectors define what a tunnel carries, and port 4500 is for NAT traversal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
question: Why does changing a KEXINIT list in transit not let a man-in-the-middle downgrade SSH's cipher choice?
options: Because KEXINIT is encrypted
Because the client ignores the server's KEXINIT
Because both KEXINIT payloads are part of the exchange hash H that the server signs, so the client's check of the signature fails
Because sequence numbers prevent any message from being changed
explain: KEXINIT is sent in the clear, but H covers both payloads. The client computes H from what it sent and received; if the attacker changed either, the server's signature over its own H will not verify on the client.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
question: After patching, a RADIUS server sends Message-Authenticator in every reply, but the switches (the NAS devices) are not configured to require it. Is Blast-RADIUS mitigated?
options: Yes, the server-side patch is sufficient
Only for EAP logins
Yes, because the switches will see a Message-Authenticator and reject replies without it automatically
Not fully: a NAS that does not require Message-Authenticator can still accept a forged reply that lacks one
explain: The forged Accept simply omits Message-Authenticator. Unless the NAS requires it, the NAS validates only the MD5 Response Authenticator, which the collision defeats. The site's advice is to upgrade servers first, then clients, and set the require flags on both sides.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: VPN leaks and TunnelVision (CVE-2024-3661): routes beat tunnels
question: Why does a VPN kill switch typically not trigger during TunnelVision?
options: Because kill switches only watch DNS
Because DHCP disables the kill switch
Because the VPN's control channel and the route to the VPN server keep working, so the client still sees a healthy connection
Because the attacker stops the VPN process
explain: Kill switches react to the tunnel going down. TunnelVision leaves the tunnel up and steers other traffic around it; the VPN server's exception route still uses the physical interface as intended.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
question: Why does Biba's strict integrity forbid a high-integrity subject from reading low-integrity data?
options: Because low data could steer the subject's actions and so corrupt what it writes to high objects
Because reading low data could reveal secrets
Because reading is slower across levels
It does not; strict integrity only restricts writes
explain: Integrity is about what you can rely on. A high subject that acts on low input can carry that contamination into high objects. Revealing secrets is a confidentiality concern, which is Bell-LaPadula's job.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
question: A laptop misses several OS patches. The engineer can still open the wiki but not code review. Which BeyondCorp component made that change, according to the 2016 paper?
options: The SSO system, by expiring the user's token
The RADIUS server, by moving the laptop to the guest network
The application, by checking the OS version itself
The Trust Inferer, by lowering the device's maximum trust tier
explain: The Trust Inferer analyses device state and sets the maximum tier; resources have minimum tiers, so the wiki (low minimum) stays available and code review (high minimum) does not. The user's identity did not change, and the application does not need its own logic.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
question: An agency patched its Ivanti appliances on the day updates appeared. Why did CISA still require resetting domain passwords twice and revoking Kerberos tickets?
options: Because the patch itself reset all passwords incorrectly
Because credentials typed through a compromised login page, and tickets issued with them, stay valid after the patch
Because Kerberos tickets expire too slowly to matter
Because the law requires annual password changes
explain: The attacker harvested credentials by modifying the login page and could have used them to obtain tickets and tokens. Patching the appliance removes the entry point, not the stolen access. Resetting twice and revoking tickets and tokens invalidates what was taken.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Running a security design review
question: A design gives an internal analytics service read access to the customer database and a direct network path to the payment processor, "for convenience". Which review question exposes the problem fastest?
options: Is the service written in a memory-safe language?
If this service is fully compromised, what can it reach and what secrets does it hold?
Does the service have a CC certificate?
Is the database encrypted at rest?
explain: Blast-radius thinking shows that one analytics bug becomes access to customer data and payments. Language choice, certification and encryption at rest matter, but none of them reveals the unnecessary path.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
question: After a timeout, a worker retries a create-ticket call and generates a new uuid4 idempotency key for each attempt. What happens?
options: Each attempt looks like a new request, so if the first call actually succeeded, the retry creates a second ticket
The API rejects uuid4 keys
Retries become safe because every key is unique
Nothing changes: idempotency keys only affect GET requests
explain: The server can only recognise a retry if it carries the same key as the original. A uuid4 is fine as a key, but it must be generated once per logical operation and reused. Stripe notes GET and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so keys there have no effect.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLMs from zero: tokens, sampling and confident mistakes
question: Your triage prompt, run 10 times at temperature 0 on the same alert, says likely_benign 9 times and likely_malicious once. What does that tell you?
options: The model is broken and should be replaced
Temperature 0 guarantees identical output, so the alert must have changed
Outputs are not fixed even at temperature 0: measure over repeated runs, and never let a single sample decide
The alert is 90% benign
explain: Inference is not fully deterministic in practice, as the Thinking Machines experiment showed. A vote of 9 to 1 is a property of the model and prompt, not a probability that the alert is benign.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
question: What made the Big Sleep and AIxCC results credible?
options: Each claim came with machine-checkable evidence: a reproducing input, a crash or a patch that passes tests
The models were very large
The vendors said so
They used the lowest temperature
explain: Verification, not model size or confidence, is what separates a finding from slop. The same standard applies to AI-written detections and code review comments.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
question: Which Morris worm door involved no programming bug at all?
options: Trusted-hosts logins and guessable passwords
fingerd reading input with gets()
sendmail's debug command
None: every door was a coding error
explain: Trusted hosts worked exactly as designed, and weak passwords are a human choice. Attack surface includes features and people, not just bugs. The fingerd and sendmail doors were implementation errors.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
question: An organisation cannot patch an old Windows Server this week. Which CISA fallback reduces the risk most?
options: Disable SMBv1 and block SMB ports at the network boundary
Turn off Windows Update
Rename the server
Pay for a larger internet connection
explain: CISA recommended disabling SMBv1 and blocking TCP 445 and related ports at the boundary when the patch could not be applied. This removes or hides the vulnerable code path.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
question: In the SSH pipeline, why match `from [0-9.]+` instead of taking a fixed word position with awk on the whole line?
options: Because lines for nonexistent users contain two extra words ('invalid user'), so the address is not always in the same position
Because grep is faster than awk
Because awk cannot read log files
Because IP addresses are encrypted in the log
explain: The 'invalid user' variant shifts every later field by two. Matching the text right after 'from' finds the address in both formats.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies
question: In the script's roadmap, what decides that 'detections + on-call' cannot start before Q3?
options: Detections are always scheduled last
Its duration is two quarters
The team has only two workstreams
It depends on central logging, which depends on the asset inventory, so the earliest start is Q3
explain: The chain inventory (Q1) then logging (Q2) then detections (Q3 and Q4) fixes the earliest start. Duration affects when it ends, not when it can begin; the team has three workstreams.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Reporting to the board: oversight duties and the annual cycle
question: A director asks for 'the number of attacks blocked each month'. What is the most useful response?
options: Provide it; directors decide what they need
Refuse, as it is confidential
Provide it with a larger number to reassure them
Explain that it measures traffic rather than risk, and offer measures tied to the top risks and their targets, such as restore time against target
explain: Blocked-attack counts rise with traffic and say nothing about exposure. Directors need effectiveness and impact measures tied to the risks they oversee; explaining why respects their question.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
question: Per the SEC's October 2024 order, what was wrong with Unisys's risk factor?
options: It disclosed too many technical details
It was filed one day late
It described cybersecurity events as hypothetical although the company knew it had suffered two SolarWinds-related intrusions
It named the attacker
explain: The SEC's point was that framing a risk as hypothetical after it had materialised misleads investors. Peirce and Uyeda disagreed with the case, but the order is the SEC's stated position.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
question: Why is passive voice especially harmful in a security recommendation?
options: It is grammatically wrong
It makes sentences too short
It hides who must act, and ownership is usually the thing that decides whether a fix happens
Executives do not understand passive voice
explain: Plain language guidance notes that passive voice obscures who handles what. In remediation, an action with no named actor is the Equifax failure in miniature.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
question: A summary lists 23 findings by severity and stops. What is it missing most?
options: A longer methodology section
Screenshots
A verdict and an ask: what the numbers mean for the decision at hand, and what the reader must decide, by when
The CVSS vectors
explain: Counts without a conclusion leave the decision-maker to do the analysis. The summary's job is to answer their question and state the decision needed.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on
question: You are not sure a pattern in a PR is exploitable. What is the best comment?
options: Block the merge until the author proves it is safe
Say nothing
A question: explain the concern and ask whether this input can ever come from a user, marked non-blocking unless the answer is yes
Mark it as an issue and Critical to be safe
explain: Questions are for uncertain concerns. Blocking on a guess burns trust; silence risks missing a bug. A clear question gets the author's knowledge on the record.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: SPIRAL trains one policy for both seats of TicTacToe with REINFORCE. Why does a single global baseline give misleading advantages?
options: The two seats have different expected returns (first-move advantage), so a global baseline credits the seat instead of the moves
A global baseline has higher variance only for single-player games
REINFORCE cannot use any baseline in multi-agent settings
The global baseline makes the game no longer zero-sum
explain: If the first player wins more often, a global baseline makes nearly every first-player move look good and every second-player move look bad. RAE subtracts a separate running mean per game and seat, so only better-than-usual play for that seat is reinforced.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: You add the user's name and the current time to the very top of the system prompt to personalize replies. What happens to the two caches?
options: Prompt caching stops working because the prefix now differs per request; the semantic cache is unaffected if it embeds only the user's question
Both stop working
Neither is affected
The semantic cache stops working; prompt caching is unaffected
explain: Prefix matching is exact from the first token, so a per-request value at the top breaks every reuse. Put stable content first and variable content last. A semantic cache keyed on the user's question does not see the system prompt, which is exactly why it needs scoping when the system prompt matters.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Question-aware and learned compression: LongLLMLingua and LLMLingua-2
question: Why can LLMLingua-2's encoder judge a word better than a causal LM scoring left to right?
options: It sees the words on both sides, so it can tell whether a word is needed by what comes after it
It is larger than any causal LM
It reads the target LLM's answer first
It computes perplexity in bits
explain: A causal LM only knows the left context: "no" at the end of "Lee and Diaz said no" is scored without knowing it is the decision. A bidirectional encoder, trained on GPT-4's keep or drop labels, uses both sides of each word.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
question: Capital One's WAF role could list and read every bucket. Which single change would have limited the damage most, even if the SSRF still worked?
options: Moving the WAF to a different AWS region
Rotating the role's credentials every hour instead of every few hours
Giving the WAF role only the permissions a firewall needs, with no S3 read access
Encrypting the HTTP traffic between the WAF and IMDS
explain: Least privilege bounds what stolen credentials can do. Faster rotation still leaves minutes to hours of valid keys, the region changes nothing, and IMDS traffic never leaves the instance, so encrypting it would not stop a relayed request.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
question: Which change most completely removes XXE and billion-laughs risk in a Java service that never uses DTDs?
options: Block requests containing the word ENTITY
Return generic error messages
Set disallow-doctype-decl to true on the parser factory
Validate the XML against a schema after parsing
explain: Without a DOCTYPE no entities can be declared, so neither external fetches nor expansion bombs are possible. Generic errors only hide the output (blind XXE still works), keyword filters are fragile, and schema validation happens after the parser has already expanded entities.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: `safe = os.path.join(BASE, name); if not safe.startswith(BASE): reject`. Which input still escapes?
options: report.txt
subdir/report.txt
An empty string
../files-backup/secret.txt when BASE is /srv/app/files
explain: join does not normalise, but even after normalising, /srv/app/files-backup/secret.txt starts with the string /srv/app/files. String prefixes are not path prefixes. Compare whole components (commonpath in Python, Path.startsWith in Java, or BASE plus a separator in Node).

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: In `tip_suggestion`, what happens when Python executes `f += sgl.gen(...)` for fork 0?
options: Python blocks until fork 0's paragraph is fully generated, then moves to fork 1
Both forks are concatenated into a single request with one long prompt
The call is submitted to fork 0's stream and returns at once, so fork 1 is submitted right away and the runtime can batch them
The function is compiled into a CUDA graph before any request is sent
explain: The interpreter runs each prompt state as an asynchronous stream: `gen` is non-blocking, like a kernel launch. Only reading a result (`forks[0]["detailed_tip"]`) waits. That is what gives intra-program parallelism.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
question: A service sends 10,000 requests, each with a different, freshly generated JSON schema, and sees much higher time to first token than with one fixed schema. What is the most likely cause?
options: The radix cache cannot store JSON outputs
Masks for unique schemas are computed on the GPU instead of the CPU
XGrammar falls back to jump-forward decoding for new schemas
Every request waits in the grammar queue for its own compilation, because the grammar cache only helps when a schema repeats
explain: Compilation is per distinct constraint and runs before the request can be scheduled. A fixed schema compiles once and then hits the cache. Reusing schemas (for example, generating them from a few templates) removes the cost.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A drone's control loop needs a filtered gyro reading every 1 ms. Someone proposes `sosfiltfilt` because it has zero phase delay. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; zero phase is ideal for control
sosfiltfilt only works on FIR filters
sosfiltfilt runs the filter backward from the end of the signal, so it needs future samples and cannot run in real time
sosfiltfilt halves the filter order, so it filters too weakly
explain: The backward pass starts from the last sample, which a real-time loop does not have yet. Real-time systems must use a causal filter (sosfilt, or an FIR) and accept or compensate its delay. Forward-backward filtering doubles the effective order; it does not halve it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: In AVX-512, `r = _mm512_mask_add_ps(src, k, a, b)` with k = 0x0003. What are lanes 0 and 5 of r?
options: Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = 0
Lane 0 = src0, lane 5 = a5 + b5
Both lanes are a + b; k only affects stores
Lane 0 = a0 + b0, lane 5 = src5
explain: 0x0003 sets bits 0 and 1, so lanes 0 and 1 get a + b. The mask_ form is merge masking: inactive lanes copy src. The maskz_ form would have produced 0 in lane 5.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: Why does a program not simply call `mmap` for every 24-byte object?
options: mmap cannot return memory smaller than a page, and each call is a system call, so it is both wasteful and slow
mmap memory cannot be written to until it is passed through malloc
mmap always returns memory on a different NUMA node
mmap regions are freed automatically after one function returns
explain: mmap works in whole pages (4 KiB on typical x86-64) and costs a kernel entry per call. An allocator amortizes both costs by carving many small objects out of one mapping. (A NUMA node, a group of CPUs with its own local memory on a non-uniform memory access machine, has nothing to do with it.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: You want to raise SGLang's KV cache budget inside a slime run. SGLang's own flag is `--mem-fraction-static`. What do you pass to slime's train.py?
options: `--sglang-mem-fraction-static 0.8`
`--mem-fraction-static 0.8`, since slime forwards unknown flags
Nothing: slime fixes SGLang memory internally
`--rollout-mem-fraction 0.8`
explain: SGLang arguments are passed through with a `--sglang-` prefix. Unprefixed flags are interpreted as Megatron or slime arguments, and there is no slime-specific rollout memory flag.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
question: A fully async agentic run sets `--eval-interval 20` and an AIME eval set, but no eval/ metrics ever appear. Why, and what should you do?
options: Eval runs only every 20 epochs
The eval set must be Parquet
--n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 0
The fully async rollout implements no evaluation, so evaluate saved checkpoints in a separate job
explain: The experiment guide and the fully async README both say the continuous queue does not implement evaluation, which would conflict with the continuously running model. Evaluate saved checkpoints separately. --n-samples-per-eval-prompt defaults to 1.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Inside the EVM: storage, calls, msg.sender and delegatecall
question: Ana calls contract A, which calls contract B. Inside B, what are msg.sender and tx.origin?
options: msg.sender = Ana, tx.origin = A
Both are Ana
Both are A
msg.sender = A, tx.origin = Ana
explain: msg.sender is the immediate caller (A); tx.origin is the EOA that signed the transaction (Ana). Authorising on tx.origin lets any contract Ana calls act as Ana.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Unchecked external calls and denial of service
question: Which line has an unchecked external call?
options: to.call{value: amt}("");
require(token.transfer(to, amt));
(bool ok, ) = to.call{value: amt}(""); require(ok);
payable(to).transfer(amt);
explain: A bare low-level call returns false on failure and execution continues. The other lines either check the result or (transfer) revert automatically.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Bridges: where many of the largest DeFi thefts happened
question: A bridge needs 5 of 9 validator signatures. The company runs 4 validators on shared infrastructure, and one partner validator has delegated signing to the company. What is the real number of compromises needed to forge a withdrawal?
options: 5 separate compromises
1: compromising the company's infrastructure reaches all 5 signatures
0, signatures cannot be forged
explain: This was Ronin's situation: one breach of Sky Mavis reached its four validators and, through the stale allowlist, the Axie DAO validator. Threshold security counts independent parties, not keys.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Incident response on chain, and where to practise
question: A team's lending contract has no pause function and no upgrade path. A bug is found that lets anyone drain 1% of funds per transaction. What can the team still do quickly?
options: Patch the contract in place
Little on chain: warn users to withdraw, ask exchanges and issuers to freeze, and coordinate with researchers; the missing pause is the real failure
Roll back the chain
Nothing at all is possible
explain: Without a pause or upgrade path the code keeps running. Response falls back to off-chain actions, which is why pause roles, caps and monitoring belong in the design.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
question: Two alerts arrive at once. Alert X: severity critical, on a test VM that holds no data, from a rule that is right 2 percent of the time. Alert Y: severity medium, on the payroll database server, from a rule that is right 40 percent of the time. Which should normally be worked first, and why?
options: Y, because priority weighs severity against asset criticality and the rule's track record, and Y wins on both
X, because critical always beats medium
Whichever arrived first
Neither until both rules are tuned
explain: Severity is only one input. Y sits on a crown-jewel asset and comes from a rule that is right far more often. That is the point of separating severity (bad if true) from priority (what to do now).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
question: A laptop's daily upload is normally about 50 MB. Today it sent 4 GB to a well-known cloud storage provider, and the company uses that provider. Which next step best separates exfiltration from normal work?
options: Close it: the provider is sanctioned
Block the provider for the whole company
Find which process and which account did the upload, and whether the destination account belongs to the company's tenant or someone else's
Geolocate the provider's IP address
explain: A sanctioned provider gives cover (T1567.002). The distinguishing facts are the process (the sync client or something odd?) and the destination tenant or account. Geolocation of a cloud provider's IP tells you where their data centre is, nothing more.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on
question: Why should a case note list what was checked and found clean?
options: To make the note longer
Because auditors only read negative results
It should not; only findings belong in a note
Because negative results bound the scope and stop others from repeating the same checks, or tell them precisely which checks to extend
explain: "No other host contacted the IP in 7 days of proxy logs" is a scope boundary. Without it, IR either repeats the search or wrongly assumes it was done more broadly.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
question: Herley argues that ignoring a piece of security advice can be rational. Which condition makes that most likely?
options: The advice costs every user effort every day, while the harm it prevents falls on a small fraction of users
The advice comes from a government agency
The advice protects against a very common attack
The advice is free to follow
explain: A daily cost multiplied across everyone easily exceeds a rare loss to a few. Advice that is cheap, or that prevents frequent and costly harm, does not fit Herley's argument.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: In CISA's description of Scattered Spider, what was the purpose of the group's first calls to a help desk?
options: To learn what steps are needed for a password reset, so later calls could follow them convincingly
To install ransomware directly
To test whether phones were monitored
To ask for a job
explain: AA23-320A says the early attempts were designed to learn the reset steps, then later calls gathered details about a target employee. Research calls are a detection opportunity if staff report them.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
question: Which change removes most of the value of a SIM swap against your employees' work accounts?
options: Asking carriers to train their staff
Requiring phishing-resistant MFA and recovery that never relies on SMS or voice
Telling employees to keep their phones charged
Using longer passwords
explain: If codes and resets never go to the phone number, moving the number gains the attacker nothing at work. Carrier rules help, but you cannot control every carrier's staff.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
question: The USB study found most people plugged in drives to find the owner. Which awareness message follows from that finding?
options: Give found devices to IT or security; they will return them safely
Never pick up anything you find
Only plug found drives into personal computers
Open only the files that look like documents
explain: The motivation was helpfulness, so the message should redirect it to a safe channel. Plugging into a personal machine still risks the person and anything that machine touches.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
question: A colleague says: 'If a model had 768 dimensions, it could track at most 768 features without errors, so superposition can't help.' What is the best reply?
options: Exact orthogonality caps it at 768, but many sparse features can share almost-orthogonal directions because they rarely fire together, and a ReLU filters small interference.
Right: superposition only works when features are dense and frequently co-occur.
Wrong: 768 dimensions can hold 768 squared exactly orthogonal directions.
Right: that is why language models need one neuron per feature.
explain: Only d directions can be exactly orthogonal, but random directions in 768 dimensions overlap by only about 0.036. When features are sparse, two overlapping features are rarely on together, and a negative bias plus ReLU removes the small leaks. Dense features make collisions common, which is when superposition stops paying.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: A residual-stream SAE and an MLP-output SAE in the same layer have the same FVU. Which do you expect to raise the language model's loss more when spliced in, and why?
options: The MLP SAE, because MLP outputs are sparser
Neither: equal FVU means equal downstream loss
The residual-stream SAE, because its error is carried into every later layer, while an MLP error is small next to the whole residual stream
The residual-stream SAE, because residual SAEs have more dead latents
explain: Gemma Scope reports consistently higher delta loss for residual-stream SAEs at similar FVU. FVU measures error relative to that site's own variance; what matters downstream is how big the error is relative to everything later layers read.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
question: You forget to drop position 0 when caching GPT-2 small activations at this site. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Many latents end up dedicated to the few huge BOS vectors, and FVU is dominated by them, while ordinary tokens reconstruct poorly
Nothing: the SAE averages over tokens, so one position cannot matter
The SAE gets more dead latents because BOS vectors are small
Training becomes faster because the BOS vectors are easy
explain: Position 0's norm here is about 38 times the others, so its squared error is over 1,000 times larger. Unnormalised, those vectors dominate the loss and the scale estimate. That is why caches skip BOS, EOS and padding.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: Two estimates at the same point: simple kriging with an assumed mean of 13.0 gives 15.090; ordinary kriging gives 15.099. Why do they differ slightly?
options: Ordinary kriging uses a different variogram
Simple kriging ignores the nearest sensor
Simple kriging's weights need not sum to 1, so the assumed mean gets weight 1 minus their sum; ordinary kriging estimates the mean from the data instead
They are numerically unstable; the difference is rounding error
explain: Simple kriging writes the estimate as $m + \sum \lambda_i (z_i - m)$, so the known mean carries the leftover weight (here $1 - 1.042$). Ordinary kriging forces the weights to sum to 1, which is equivalent to using a data-estimated mean (12.80 here).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: A teammate 'simplifies' the sampler: on rejection, sample the replacement from p instead of the residual. What happens?
options: Nothing; p and the residual are the same distribution
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft under-proposes, because their accepted mass is counted twice
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft over-proposes
Acceptance rate drops but outputs stay exact
explain: Rejection still happens with probability 0.3 in the toy example, but the replacement now follows p, so each token gets min(p, q) + 0.3 p(x): 0.45, 0.26, 0.16, 0.13 instead of 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. 'a' and 'dog', which the draft over-proposes, gain mass. The residual sends rejected mass only to under-covered tokens, adding exactly the missing p(x) - q(x).

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
question: On the Slaney mel scale, which span covers more mel units: 0 to 1000 Hz or 4000 to 8000 Hz?
options: 0 to 1000 Hz (15 mel versus about 10.1 mel)
4000 to 8000 Hz, because it is four times wider in Hz
They are equal, because the scale is logarithmic everywhere
It depends on the number of mel bands
explain: 0 to 1000 Hz is the linear part: 15 mel. 4000 to 8000 Hz is one doubling in the log region: 27 ln 2 / ln 6.4, about 10.1 mel. So the filterbank spends more bands on the lowest kilohertz, where vowels and pitch live, than on the top four kilohertz. The number of bands only decides how finely the axis is cut.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: Window 1 predicts its last complete segment ends at 28.00 s, but the speaker actually finished it at 27.40 s and started a new sentence. What does buffered long-form transcription do next?
options: Starts window 2 at 30.00 s, as always
Starts window 2 at 28.00 s and may skip the words spoken between 27.40 and 28.00 s
Re-runs window 1 with a higher temperature
Averages the two timestamps and starts at 27.70 s
explain: The seek position follows the predicted timestamp, so window 2 starts at 28.00 s and the 600 ms after the true boundary is never transcribed. This is the error propagation between windows that the paper warns about.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: Why is calling munmap on a small buffer often slower in a 64-thread process than in a single-threaded one?
options: The kernel must shoot down stale TLB entries on every CPU running the process, using IPIs and waiting for them
munmap must zero the pages first
Each thread has its own page table that must be edited
munmap takes a global lock across all processes
explain: Threads share one page table, so any CPU running one of them might cache the translation. The initiating CPU interrupts those CPUs and waits for them to flush before the pages can be reused. Threads do not have separate page tables, and freed pages are not zeroed at munmap.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: You build a CAA vector from 300 pairs where every positive prompt happens to be longer than its negative partner. What is the most likely problem?
options: None: averaging over 300 pairs removes all confounds
The vector partly encodes prompt length, because that difference is consistent across pairs and does not average out
The vector will have length zero
Mean difference only works with exactly one pair
explain: Averaging cancels differences that vary randomly across pairs. A difference that is the same in every pair, such as length, survives averaging and becomes part of the vector. CAA avoids this by making each pair identical except for one answer letter.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
question: Your hook does `h[:, start:] += vec` where start is the prompt's post-instruction position. Scores look right, but generated text is identical to the unsteered model after the first token. What is wrong?
options: The vector has the wrong sign
Generation recomputes the vector from scratch each step
The model normalizes the vector away at the final layer
With the KV cache each decoding step passes one position, so the slice from start is empty and nothing is added
explain: The first forward pass covers the whole prompt, where the slice works. Later steps see a tensor of length 1, and slicing from a start index of, say, 60 selects nothing. Add to every position when the sequence length is 1, or track absolute positions.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 6 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
options: 6: Kafka splits each partition across consumers
1: only the group leader reads
4: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so 2 sit idle
12: every consumer reads every partition
explain: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group. With more consumers than partitions, the extras get nothing. Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Which problem of the basic RNN encoder-decoder did Bahdanau-style attention fix, and which did it leave in place?
options: It fixed sequential computation but kept the fixed-length vector
It removed the fixed-length vector bottleneck but kept the sequential recurrent chain
It fixed both, which is why the Transformer only changed the training recipe
It fixed neither; it only made the model more interpretable
explain: The decoder could now look at every encoder state through a weighted sum, so the single fixed vector stopped being a bottleneck. The encoder and decoder were still RNNs, so computation inside a sequence stayed sequential. The Transformer removed that remaining chain.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
question: You remove the positional encodings from a trained encoder and feed it "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". What happens to the encoder output for the token "man"?
options: It is identical in both sentences
It differs, because attention weights depend on which tokens are nearby
It differs, because the FFN processes positions in order
It becomes all zeros
explain: Without positional information, self-attention and the position-wise FFN are permutation equivariant. Both sentences contain the same three tokens, so "man" gets the same output in each. That is why order must be injected explicitly.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: You increase the context length of a model from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens and keep d fixed. Roughly how does the score-matrix work per layer change?
options: It grows about 4 times, like the FFN
It grows about 16 times, while the FFN work grows about 4 times
It stays the same because heads run in parallel
It grows about 2 times
explain: Score work scales with n^2: (16384/4096)^2 = 16. The FFN and projections scale with n, so they grow 4 times. Parallel heads change wall-clock time, not the amount of work.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: the full RSJ weight and query term counts
question: After feedback on the query cheap flights, which situation gives cheap a negative RSJ weight?
options: Cheap appears in more than half of the whole collection
Cheap appears in all of the relevant documents
Cheap appears in a smaller share of the relevant documents than of the other documents
Cheap appears in exactly one relevant document
explain: The weight is the log of (odds of t among relevant) over (odds of t among the rest). It is negative when t is relatively rarer in relevant documents. Appearing in over half the collection drives the no-judgment IDF negative, but with judgments what matters is the comparison. One relevant document out of four (25%) against 20% elsewhere still gave +0.538.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Fields measured, and what is fixed at index time
question: An eager-scoring index (stored BM25 impacts) receives 20% more documents, mostly about a new topic. What goes stale in the stored scores of the old documents?
options: Nothing, because each stored score only depends on its own document
Only the term counts
N, the document frequencies and avgdl, so every stored IDF and length factor is now slightly off
Only the scores of documents longer than avgdl
explain: A stored impact bakes in IDF (from N and n_t) and the length factor (from avgdl). New documents change all three, so old impacts drift until they are recomputed. A query-time scorer reads fresh statistics on every query.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights
question: Your from-scratch GPT-2 small reports 163,037,184 parameters. What did you most likely get wrong?
options: The MLP is 8 times wider than the embedding, not 4
You counted the attention mask buffers as parameters
lm_head has its own weight matrix instead of sharing wte's
The position table has 2,048 rows instead of 1,024
explain: The excess is 163,037,184 - 124,439,808 = 38,597,376 = 50,257 x 768, exactly one extra token-sized matrix. That is an untied lm_head. A doubled position table would add only 786,432, and buffers are not parameters.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: You have 4 GPUs, micro-batch B = 16, T = 1024, and want build-nanogpt's 524,288 tokens per optimizer step. How many micro-steps must each GPU accumulate?
explain: 524,288 / (16 x 1024 x 4) = 8. Each GPU runs 8 micro-steps, all-reducing only on the last one, and the 4 GPUs together cover 524,288 tokens.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
question: A density is $p(x) = 2x$ on $[0, 1]$ and 0 elsewhere. What is the probability that $x$ lands in $[0, 0.5]$?
options: 0.5, because the range is half of [0, 1]
1, because p(0.5) = 1
0.75, because the density is larger on the right half
explain: The probability is the area $\int_0^{0.5} 2x\,dx = x^2$ evaluated from 0 to 0.5, which is $0.25$. The density's value at a point, $p(0.5) = 1$, is not a probability. Half the range gets only a quarter of the area because the density is low near 0. Check: $\int_0^1 2x\,dx = 1$, so this is a valid density.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
question: A loss is roughly quadratic near its minimum, with Hessian eigenvalues 50, 10 and 0.5. What is the largest stable learning rate for plain gradient descent, and which direction will be slowest?
options: 2/0.5 = 4; the 50 direction is slowest
1/50 = 0.02; all directions converge at the same speed
2/50 = 0.04; the direction with eigenvalue 0.5 is slowest
2/10 = 0.2, using the middle eigenvalue
explain: Stability needs $|1 - \eta\lambda| < 1$ for every eigenvalue, so $\eta < 2/50 = 0.04$. At $\eta = 0.04$ the 0.5 direction shrinks by $1 - 0.02 = 0.98$ per step, very slowly. The condition number $50/0.5 = 100$ measures this mismatch.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: A script runs `for f in $(ls *.txt); do wc -l $f; done` in a folder containing `notes.txt` and `q3 report.txt`. What happens?
options: It works: the glob keeps each file name intact
wc is called on `notes.txt`, `q3` and `report.txt`, and fails on the last two
bash refuses to run because ls output cannot be expanded
Only `notes.txt` is processed because the loop stops at the first space
explain: The command substitution `$(ls *.txt)` is unquoted, so its output is word-split on whitespace, and `q3 report.txt` becomes two words. The fix is to let the glob produce the list directly: `for f in *.txt; do wc -l "$f"; done`. Globbing results are not split again.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
question: Why does `grep -c '.' notes.txt` count every line except the empty ones?
options: `.` matches a literal dot, and most lines end with one
grep skips empty lines in every search
`-c` counts characters, not lines
`.` matches any single character, so any line with at least one character matches
explain: In a regex, `.` is any one character, and a line matches if the pattern matches anywhere in it. Every non-empty line qualifies and only empty lines fail: a real run on the lines `ab`, an empty line and `c` prints 2. To match a literal dot, escape it: `'\.'`.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: Why do the dense vectors let a model generalize from cat to kitten when one-hot codes do not?
options: Dense vectors have more dimensions, so they hold more information
The dot product of two one-hot vectors is undefined
Nearby inputs produce nearby activations, so what the network learned for one word partly applies to the other
Dense vectors are normalized to length 1
explain: The downstream layers are smooth functions of their input. If kitten's vector is close to cat's, the network's output for kitten is close to its output for cat. One-hot codes have more dimensions, not fewer, and their dot products are well defined (just always 0).

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: Your search for words similar to *cheap* returns *expensive* near the top. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Antonyms share most of their contexts (prices, tickets, very), so distributional training places them close
A bug: cosine similarity must be negative for antonyms
The vectors were not normalized before training
Negative sampling inverts antonym vectors
explain: The objective only sees contexts. *Cheap* and *expensive* appear around the same words, so their vectors align. Nothing in SGNS or GloVe pushes antonyms to negative cosine.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
question: A linear autoencoder with a 2-number code, trained with squared error, reaches exactly the reconstruction error of 2-component PCA on your data. What does this tell you?
options: The autoencoder found the same 2-d subspace PCA keeps, as theory predicts for a linear decoder and squared error
The autoencoder overfit and memorized the training points
Autoencoders are always equivalent to PCA, even with nonlinear layers
The code is the same two numbers PCA would give for every point
explain: With a linear decoder and squared error, an undercomplete autoencoder spans PCA's principal subspace. It can use any basis of that subspace, so its code numbers need not equal PCA's coordinates. Nonlinear autoencoders can do more than PCA.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
question: A kernel author shrinks the output tile from 128 x 128 to 64 x 64, keeping K the same. What happens to each tile's arithmetic intensity?
options: Nothing changes: intensity depends only on M, N and K
It doubles, because smaller tiles fit better in shared memory
The total FLOPs of the GEMM halve
It halves, from 64 to 32 FLOP/B against the memory feeding the tile
explain: Intensity of a tile is T/2 FLOP/B, so halving T halves it: each loaded value is reused 64 times instead of 128. The GEMM's total FLOPs (2MNK) do not change; only how often each byte is reused on chip.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor
question: A team serving a 70B model at batch 1 moves from 4 to 8 tensor-parallel GPUs and sees per-token latency fall only about 25%. What is the most likely reason?
options: The weights no longer fit in memory
Pipeline bubbles appear when T exceeds 4
Each GPU's share of weight reads halved, but the fixed per-layer all-reduce latency and other per-step costs did not, so they now dominate
NVLink bandwidth is saturated by the 16 KiB activations
explain: The bandwidth term halves with T, but 160 all-reduces per token cost roughly the same at any T, as do kernel launches. Moving 16 KiB over 600 GB/s takes tens of nanoseconds, so bandwidth is not the limit; latency is.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
question: Using the same compiled code, how many instructions does the CPU execute for sum(a, 1000)?
explain: 5 instructions run once before the loop (test, jle, two xors, the padding nop), the 4-instruction loop body runs 1000 times, and retq runs once: 5 + 4000 + 1 = 4006. Instruction count grows with n because the loop body is re-fetched and re-executed each iteration.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Which of these operations has to go through a system call?
options: Reading bytes from a file
Adding two numbers in registers
Calling a function defined in your own program
Writing to a local variable on the stack
explain: Arithmetic, function calls and stack accesses are ordinary user-mode instructions on the process's own memory. A file lives on a device that only the kernel may touch, so read() must trap into the kernel.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
question: Two pages have Jaccard similarity 0.5 over their 5-gram shingles. With FineWeb's 14 buckets of 8 hashes, how likely are they to be flagged as duplicates?
options: About 50 percent, because MinHash estimates Jaccard directly
Always, because they share half their shingles
Never, because MinHash only catches exact copies
About 5 percent, because all 8 hashes must agree in some bucket
explain: One bucket matches with probability 0.5 to the 8th, about 0.0039. The chance at least one of 14 buckets matches is 1 - (1 - 0.0039)^14, about 0.053. Banding turns the per-hash match rate into a sharp threshold near 0.7 (a 50 percent chance at s of about 0.69).

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
question: Someone proposes using each sampled response's own reward as its baseline, b = r(y). What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; any baseline keeps the gradient unbiased
The variance increases but the policy still learns the right thing
The advantage r(y) - b is always zero, so the policy never learns
The gradient becomes biased toward longer responses
explain: The unbiasedness argument needs b to be independent of the sampled response. With b = r(y) every advantage is exactly 0 and every update vanishes. Valid baselines depend on the state (like V(s)) or on the other samples for the same prompt, not on the sample being scored. GRPO's group mean also includes the scored sample, a small bias that shrinks as the group grows.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
question: A team lowercases text when indexing but forgets to lowercase queries. A user searches for Deploy. What happens on our six documents?
options: It matches d2, d3 and d5 as expected
It matches every document, because the lookup falls back to a scan
It matches nothing, because the dictionary contains deploy but not Deploy
It matches only d3, the document that starts with roll
explain: The dictionary is an exact lookup structure. Index-time and query-time analysis must agree, or terms simply miss. Search libraries let you configure one analyzer (the chain of tokenize and normalize steps) and apply it on both sides for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: A term occurs in all N documents of the collection. How much does it contribute to any TF-IDF score using idf = log(N/df)?
options: Nothing, because its idf is log(1) = 0
A lot, because it has the highest tf
It depends on the base of the logarithm
It contributes its raw tf
explain: N/df = 1 and log(1) = 0 in every base, so the term has zero weight whatever its tf. idf turns such terms into automatic stop words for scoring, which is why the in our example stops dominating.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
options: two three
two
one two three
two three other
explain: switch jumps to case 2, then falls through into case 3 because nothing stops it, and the break after three leaves the switch before default. Forgetting break is a classic bug; when fallthrough is intended, write a comment saying so.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `char a[] = "cat", b[] = "cat";` Does `if (a == b)` take the branch?
options: Yes, the two strings hold the same characters
It does not compile
Only if the compiler merges identical strings
No: == compares the addresses of two different arrays; use strcmp(a, b) == 0
explain: Both arrays decay to pointers to their first elements, and two distinct arrays never share an address, so the comparison is false; clang even warns `array comparison always evaluates to false`. strcmp compares the characters and returns 0 when they match.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
question: What does `int *f(int);` declare, compared with `int (*f)(int);`?
options: Both declare a pointer to a function returning int
The first is a pointer to an int, the second a function
Both declare a function returning a pointer
The first declares a function returning int *; the second, a pointer to a function returning int
explain: Without parentheses, `()` binds to f first, so f is a function (taking int) that returns `int *`. With `(*f)`, f is first a pointer, and what it points to is a function taking int and returning int.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
question: You add a variant `Triangle { b: f64, h: f64 }` to `Shape` but do not touch `area`. What happens?
options: `area` returns 0.0 for a triangle, the default for an unmatched value
It compiles with a warning and panics when a triangle reaches the match
The match falls through to the next arm, as a C switch without break does
rustc rejects the program with E0004, because the match no longer covers every variant
explain: Matches are exhaustive and checked at compile time. Adding a variant makes every match on the type that lacks it (and lacks a `_` arm) a compile error, which points you at each place that needs a decision. There is no default value and no fall-through.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
question: `v` is a `Vec<String>` with three elements. Which line compiles on its own?
options: `let s = v[1];`
`for s in v {}` followed by `println!("{}", v.len());`
`let s: &String = &v[1];`
`let first = &v[0]; v.push(String::new()); println!("{first}");`
explain: Borrowing an element is fine. Option 1 is E0507 (cannot move out of an index). Option 2 is E0382, because the loop consumed `v`. Option 4 is E0502: `first` is still used after `push` needs `&mut v`.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
question: A tree where each child needs a pointer back to its parent, and nodes are created and removed while the program runs. Which choice fits best?
options: Plain `&Node` references stored in each child
`Rc` from parent to children and `Weak` from child to parent (with `RefCell` where nodes must change)
Clone the parent into each child
explain: Nodes have no single owner whose scope covers every use, which is what plain references need. Cloning would give each child a separate copy rather than the real parent. `Rc` counts owners; a `Weak` back-pointer does not count, so parent and child do not keep each other alive in a cycle that leaks. `RefCell` allows mutation, checked at run time. This is the Book's tree design.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
question: $A$ has shape $3 \times 5$. Which input can it multiply, and what comes out?
options: A vector with 5 components; out comes a vector with 3
A vector with 3 components; out comes a vector with 5
Any vector; out comes a 3 x 5 matrix
A vector with 15 components; out comes a scalar
explain: Each row has 5 entries and is dotted with $\mathbf{x}$, so $\mathbf{x}$ needs 5 components. There are 3 rows, so 3 output components. An $m \times n$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
question: After a least-squares fit, the residual is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}$. Which statement must hold?
options: r is the zero vector
r points in the same direction as y
r is orthogonal to every column of X
r has the same length as y
explain: The best fit is the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space, so the leftover is perpendicular to that space: $X^\top\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$. It is zero only if $\mathbf{y}$ was already reachable, which a tall noisy system almost never is.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: A classifier gives the correct class probability 0.9 on one example and 0.1 on another. Roughly how do their cross-entropy losses compare?
options: The 0.1 example costs about 22 times more (2.303 vs 0.105)
They are equal, since both are 0.4 away from 0.5
The 0.1 example costs exactly 9 times more
The 0.9 example costs more because it is more confident
explain: Cross-entropy is $-\ln p$: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$ and $-\ln 0.1 = 2.303$, a ratio of about 22. The log makes the cost grow without bound as the probability of the right answer goes to 0, which is exactly the confident-wrong case.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
question: You can't change the degree-9 model. Which change most directly reduces its overfitting?
options: Train longer to reach exactly zero training loss
Collect more training data from the same distribution
Evaluate on the training set instead
Increase the learning rate
explain: More data constrains the same model: median test RMS fell from 0.643 at N = 10 to 0.340 at N = 100. Training longer only drives it further into the noise, and evaluating on training data hides the problem.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
question: You ran 5-fold cross-validation to choose lambda, picked the best value, and want to report expected performance. What should you report?
options: The mean cross-validation score of the chosen lambda
The best single fold's score
The training score of the final model
The score on a test set that was never used for choosing lambda
explain: The chosen lambda won partly by luck on those folds, so its cross-validation score is optimistic. The scikit-learn guide keeps a test set aside for exactly this final evaluation.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
question: Connect-the-dots approximation of $\sin x$ gave worst errors 0.21, 0.070 and 0.019 with 4, 8 and 16 equal pieces. Roughly how many pieces give a worst error near 0.005?
explain: Each doubling cut the error by about 3 to 4 times, and the ratio was heading toward 4. One more doubling, to 32 pieces, gives about 0.0048. 64 would overshoot to around 0.0012.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
question: A 10-class network gives the true class probability 0.98 and some wrong class probability 0.015. What are $\partial L/\partial z$ for those two logits?
options: 0 and 0, because the prediction is already right
explain: $\partial L/\partial z_j = p_j - \delta_{yj}$. True class: 0.98 - 1 = -0.02, a small push up. Wrong class: 0.015 - 0 = 0.015, a small push down. Confident correct predictions produce small gradients, but never exactly zero.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has stopped falling and is slowly rising. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Train for many more epochs until validation loss falls again
Report test accuracy at every epoch and pick the best one
Increase the model size
Stop at the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping) or add regularisation
explain: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is the signature of overfitting. Early stopping or weight decay from the ML fundamentals course address it. Picking the epoch by test accuracy leaks the test set into model selection.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
question: A database scans a 50-page table in a loop, over and over, and has 49 frames for it. Which replacement policy gives the best hit rate?
options: LRU, because it keeps recently used pages
FIFO, because the scan is in arrival order
Random, because LRU and FIFO always evict the page needed next and hit 0% of the time
All three give the same hit rate
explain: In a loop larger than the cache, the least recently used page is exactly the one the loop needs next, so LRU (and FIFO, which evicts in the same order here) misses on every access. Random sometimes keeps the right pages and gets a non-zero hit rate. OPT would do better still.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: Thread A starts thread B and then sets `cfg = load_config()`. Thread B begins by reading `cfg->port`. It crashes occasionally. What kind of bug is this, and what is the usual fix?
options: An atomicity violation; wrap the read of cfg->port in a lock
An order violation; make B wait on a condition variable until A sets a flag after loading cfg
A deadlock; acquire locks in a global order
A data race on port; declare cfg volatile
explain: B assumes A's assignment has already happened: the intended order is not enforced. A lock alone does not fix it, since B could still take the lock first and see NULL. B must wait for a state variable (set by A after loading) using a condition variable, as in OSTEP's Mozilla fix. volatile does not create ordering.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: In data journaling, why must the file system wait for TxB, I[v2], B[v2] and Db to finish before writing TxE, instead of issuing all five writes at once?
options: Because the disk can only accept one write at a time
Because TxE must be written to the final location, not the journal
Because the disk may reorder a large write; TxE could land before Db, and replay would then copy garbage as if it were committed
Because waiting makes the journal smaller
explain: Disks schedule writes internally. If all five are issued together, TxE might hit the disk while Db has not. After a crash the transaction looks committed, and recovery would checkpoint garbage. Writing TxE only after the rest completes, as an atomic 512-byte write, closes the window.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
question: A language model gives probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.1 to three successive tokens, each conditioned on the tokens before it. What is the total log-probability (natural log) of the three tokens?
options: About -4.61, the sum of the three logs, equal to ln 0.01
About -1.54, the average of the three logs
0.8, the sum of the three probabilities
About -2.30, the log of the smallest probability
explain: By the chain rule the joint probability is 0.2 x 0.5 x 0.1 = 0.01, and the log of a product is the sum of logs: -1.61 - 0.69 - 2.30 = -4.61. The average, -1.54 per token, is minus the cross-entropy per token used as a training loss.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood
question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
